title: Kievan Rus'
titleline: Kievan Rus' - The History Web
para1: Kievan Rus'. Kievan Rus' (c. 880-1240) was the first great state of the East Slavs - the ancestor of Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus alike, and the arena where the Vikings met Byzantium. Its founders were Norse warriors and traders, the Rus, who made themselves masters of the river routes between the Baltic and the Black Sea; around 882 the Varangian prince Oleg the Wise extended his power from Novgorod south along the Dnieper and took Kiev, which remained the capital for three and a half centuries.
para2: The turning point came in 988, when the prince of Kiev accepted Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium: the Rus were baptized in the Dnieper, and the faith, the alphabet, and the art of Constantinople flowed north. At its height under Yaroslav the Wise (1019-1054), Kievan Rus' stretched from the White Sea to the Black Sea and from the Carpathians to the Taman Peninsula; Yaroslav's sons issued its first written law code, the Russkaya Pravda. It was Vladimir the Great (980-1015) who had spread Christianity by decree through Kiev and beyond - the baptism that defined the Rus' world.
para3: But the dynasty divided what it conquered: the custom of splitting the realm among the ruler's sons splintered Rus' into rival principalities, and the center of gravity drifted northeast to Vladimir and the forests. Then came the catastrophe: in 1237-1241 the Mongol armies of Batu Khan swept through the principalities, and in December 1240 they stormed and burned Kiev itself.
para4: Kievan Rus' died under the Mongol yoke - but its heritage divided three ways: the northeast principalities became Muscovy and Russia, the western lands fell to Lithuania and Poland and became Ukraine and Belarus, and the memory of a single baptized Rus' - Kiev's golden age - became the founding myth of all three.

title: The Carolingian Empire
titleline: The Carolingian Empire - The History Web
para1: The Carolingian Empire. The Carolingian Empire (800-888) was medieval Europe's first attempt to rebuild the Roman Empire in the West - the realm of Charlemagne, the most important European ruler between Rome's fall and the modern age. The Carolingian family had risen as mayors of the palace under the Merovingian kings; Pepin the Short took the crown itself in 751, and his son Charles - Charlemagne, 'Charles the Great' - spent a forty-six-year reign (768-814) conquering: the Lombards of Italy, the Saxons in wars and rebellions that ran from 772 to 804, the Avars, and the Spanish March - with his one great defeat coming at Roncevaux Pass in 778.
para2: On Christmas Day 800, in Rome, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans. The coronation was a revolution: it declared that the West had an emperor of its own again, answerable to no one in Constantinople - and it bound the Frankish monarchy and the papacy into the partnership that would shape medieval Europe. From his capital at Aachen, Charlemagne governed an empire of 10 to 20 million people, issued laws, reformed the currency, and sponsored the 'Carolingian Renaissance' - a revival of learning that preserved much of classical Latin literature.
para3: The empire could not outlive its founder's line. Charlemagne's son Louis the Pious could not hold his own sons together; after his death, civil war ended at the Treaty of Verdun (843), which split the empire into three kingdoms - the seeds of France and Germany. Charles the Fat briefly reunited the whole in 884, but he was deposed in 887 and died in 888, and the empire dissolved for good.
para4: The Carolingian experiment failed as a state - and succeeded as an idea. The memory of a united Christian Europe under one emperor haunted the Middle Ages: the Holy Roman Empire claimed Charlemagne's mantle, France and Germany both claim his inheritance, and modern Europeans still call him the father of Europe.

title: The Crown of Aragon
titleline: The Crown of Aragon - The History Web
para1: The Crown of Aragon. The Crown of Aragon was medieval Spain's other great power - and the opposite of Castile in almost every way. Born in 1162 of the union between the Kingdom of Aragon and the County of Barcelona, it was a 'composite monarchy': a family of lands - Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia, and later Majorca, Sicily, Sardinia, and Naples - each keeping its own laws, parliaments, and privileges under one king.
para2: Where Castile expanded south into al-Andalus, Aragon expanded east into the sea. Its kings - above all James I the Conqueror, who took Majorca (1231) and Valencia (1238-1245) - and its Catalan merchants and sailors built a great Mediterranean empire: Sardinia was conquered between 1324 and 1420, and for a time the Crown even held parts of Greece. Barcelona became one of the great trading cities of Europe, and at its height in the 14th and 15th centuries the Crown was a thalassocracy - a sea-power ruling the Balearics, Sicily, Corsica, Sardinia, Malta, and, from 1442, southern Italy itself.
para3: The Crown of Aragon stood early for limited monarchy: it was officially 'a feudal monarchy subject to the fueros' - the chartered liberties of each land - and its parliaments, the Corts of Aragon, Catalonia, and Valencia, were among the most powerful in medieval Europe.
para4: In 1469 Ferdinand II of Aragon married Isabella of Castile, and their grandson inherited both crowns. Aragon's distinct identity persisted within Spain until the 18th century, when the Bourbons abolished its institutions after the War of the Spanish Succession. But Catalonia's memory of its medieval Mediterranean empire - and of its lost liberties - is still very much alive.

title: The Crown of Castile
titleline: The Crown of Castile - The History Web
para1: The Crown of Castile. The Crown of Castile was the powerhouse of the Reconquista and the foundation of Spain. Castile began as the frontier land of castles facing Muslim al-Andalus, and in 1230 was permanently united with Leon under Ferdinand III, who had inherited Castile in 1217 and Leon in 1230. From its Meseta heartland, Castile led the great 13th-century advance south: Ferdinand III himself conquered the Guadalquivir valley - Cordoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248 - and his son Alfonso X added Murcia, leaving Muslim rule confined to Granada. Castilian kings piled kingdom into their titles: 'King of Castile, Leon, Toledo, Galicia, Murcia, Jaen, Cordoba, Seville...'
para2: Castile was a warrior society organized for frontier war - and a precocious political one: its Cortes, with nobles, clergy, and representatives of the towns sitting as three estates, became one of medieval Europe's earliest parliaments, and its language - Castilian - spread with its conquests to become what the world now calls Spanish.
para3: The 15th century made Castile the center of a world power. The marriage of Isabella I of Castile to Ferdinand II of Aragon in 1469 joined the two great Spanish crowns; in 1492 their armies took Granada, ending Muslim rule in Spain, and in the same year Castile - and Castile alone, in law - sponsored Columbus and claimed the Americas. Within a generation, Castilian conquistadors had destroyed the Aztec and Inca empires, and silver from Castile's American empire made it the greatest power in Europe.
para4: Yet Castile remained legally distinct even within a united Spain - with its own laws, Cortes, and administration - until the Bourbon reforms of the 18th century dissolved the old crowns into a single Spanish state. Modern Spain is, in language and institutions, above all Castile's child.

title: The First & Second Bulgarian Empires
titleline: The First & Second Bulgarian Empires - The History Web
para1: The First and Second Bulgarian Empires. Bulgaria was the great power of the medieval Balkans - twice. The First Bulgarian Empire (681-1018) was founded when the Bulgar khan Asparuh led his people south of the Danube and defeated Byzantium, carving out the first state in Europe the empire had to recognize. Under Krum - who killed a Byzantine emperor in battle and prepared a full siege of Constantinople itself - under Boris I the Bulgarians accepted Orthodox Christianity (864) - a choice that decided the religious map of Eastern Europe - and under Simeon I (893-927), who took the title tsar (caesar) and crushed the Byzantines at the Achelous in 917, the empire reached its golden age: Old Church Slavonic became its official language in 893, and the capital Preslav became the center of a new Slavic Christian culture.
para2: Byzantium's revenge came under Basil II, the 'Bulgar-Slayer,' who at Kleidion in 1014 captured 14,000 Bulgarians and is said to have blinded 99 of every 100: after a generation of war, the First Empire was extinguished in 1018, and Bulgaria spent 167 years as a Byzantine province. Then, in 1185, the brothers Asen and Peter rose in revolt and founded the Second Bulgarian Empire, with its capital at Tarnovo.
para3: The Second Empire's century was dazzling and brief: under Kaloyan - who crushed the Crusaders' Latin Empire at Adrianople in 1205 and took its emperor prisoner - and Ivan Asen II, who defeated the Despotate of Epirus, Bulgaria again dominated the Balkans, ruling from the Adriatic to the Black Sea, some 300,000 square kilometers. Until 1256 the Second Empire was the dominant power in the Balkans.
para4: But the rising Ottoman Turks swallowed the Balkans piecemeal: Tarnovo fell in 1393, and by 1396 the Second Empire was gone. Bulgaria disappeared from the map of nations for nearly five centuries - yet its two empires left Eastern Europe its alphabet, its church, and the memory that made modern Bulgaria possible.

title: The Frankish Kingdom (Merovingians)
titleline: The Frankish Kingdom (Merovingians) - The History Web
para1: The Frankish Kingdom (Merovingians). The Merovingians were the first royal dynasty of France - the 'long-haired kings' who ruled the Franks for two and a half centuries (481-751) and turned a tribe of the Roman frontier into the greatest power in Western Europe. They take their name from the semi-legendary Merovech, but the dynasty's real founder was Clovis I: succeeding his father Childeric in 481, he destroyed the last Roman rump state in Gaul at Soissons (486), broke the Alamanni at Tolbiac (496), and crushed the Visigoths at Vouille (507).
para2: Clovis's most consequential act was his conversion: while other Germanic kings were Arian heretics, Clovis accepted Catholic Christianity, winning him the loyalty of the Gallo-Roman bishops and people - and laying the foundation of the ancient alliance between the Frankish crown and the Church. By his death in 511 the Franks held nearly all of Gaul; his name, in its later form 'Louis,' would be borne by French kings for thirteen hundred years.
para3: Yet the dynasty's own customs weakened it: Frankish kings divided the realm among their sons like private property, and the partitioned kingdoms - Austrasia, Neustria, Burgundy, Aquitaine - wasted themselves in civil wars between royal brothers. Power drained from the sacred, long-haired kings (a shorn Merovingian could not reign) to their chief ministers, the mayors of the palace.
para4: The mayors - the Carolingian family - became the real rulers of Francia: Charles Martel ruled without a king on the throne at all from 737 to 741. In 751 his son Pepin the Short finished the logic of a century: he deposed the last Merovingian, Childeric III, cut his hair, and took the crown with the Church's blessing. The Merovingians passed into legend - the dynasty that had made the Franks a great power, and made France possible.

title: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania
titleline: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania - The History Web
para1: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania. The Grand Duchy of Lithuania was Europe's last pagan state - and for a time its largest country. Its founder Mindaugas united the Baltic tribes and was crowned king in 1253, holding off the crusading Teutonic and Livonian Orders. Under Gediminas and his sons Algirdas and Kestutis in the 14th century, the duchy exploded eastward over the ruins of Kievan Rus', ruling most of today's Belarus and Ukraine from its new capital, Vilnius (from 1323) - a pagan warrior elite governing a vast Orthodox Slavic realm, in constant war with the Teutonic Order, which it fenced off with a castle network along the Nemunas river.
para2: The duchy's turning point was the Union of Krewo (1385-1386): the grand duke Jogaila married the young queen of Poland, accepted baptism - Europe's last pagan ruler converted - and joined the two states in dynastic union. Under his cousin Vytautas the Great, Lithuania reached its greatest extent, and in 1410 Lithuanian and Polish arms together crushed the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald, one of the greatest battles of medieval Europe.
para3: Union with Poland slowly pulled Lithuania into the Polish orbit: the Lithuanian nobility Polonized, and pressure from rising Moscow made separation impossible. In 1569 the Union of Lublin fused the two states into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth - though Lithuania kept its own laws, army, treasury, and administration within it.
para4: The Commonwealth was partitioned out of existence in 1795, and Lithuania vanished into the Russian Empire. The grand duchy's memory is the foundation of modern Lithuania's statehood - and its centuries ruling the old lands of Rus' are woven into the history of Belarus and Ukraine too.

title: The Grand Duchy of Moscow
titleline: The Grand Duchy of Moscow - The History Web
para1: The Grand Duchy of Moscow. Muscovy rose from nothing: in 1263 Moscow was a minor appanage town, given to Daniel, youngest son of Alexander Nevsky. Within two centuries it had swallowed its rivals, thrown off the Mongol yoke, and become the core of Russia - the most improbable rise in medieval Europe.
para2: Moscow's princes succeeded by cunning more than valor. They served the Mongol khans as tribute-collectors - Ivan I (1325-1340), called 'Moneybag,' grew rich gathering the khan's taxes from the other Russian princes - and they won over the Church: the seat of the Russian metropolitan moved to Moscow, making it the spiritual as well as political center of the Russian lands. Prince by prince, 'the gathering of the Russian lands' went on.
para3: The defiance began under Dmitry Donskoy, who in 1380 inflicted a milestone defeat on the Tatars and permanently joined the grand principality of Vladimir to Moscow. The liberation was completed under Ivan III (1462-1505), who formally annexed Novgorod in 1478, absorbed nearly all the Russian states, and took the title 'sovereign of all Russia'; his defeat of the Tatars in 1480 traditionally marks the end of Tatar suzerainty, after which he styled himself autocrat. He laid claim to the whole legacy of Kievan Rus' - a claim that brought Moscow into conflict with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Meanwhile the Russian Church had declared its independence (autocephaly) in 1448, and the fall of Constantinople in 1453 left Moscow the capital of the Orthodox world.
para4: In 1547 Ivan IV - 'the Terrible' - was crowned not grand prince but Tsar of all Russia: Muscovy had become the Tsardom of Russia. The little principality on the Moskva river had become, in three centuries, the largest state in Europe.

title: The Kingdom of Bohemia
titleline: The Kingdom of Bohemia - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Bohemia. The Kingdom of Bohemia was the Czech crown - the state of the Premyslid dukes raised to royalty within the Holy Roman Empire. Though earlier dukes had worn personal crowns, the hereditary kingdom was established in 1198 by Ottokar I and confirmed by Frederick II's Golden Bull of Sicily in 1212: the Czech king was freed from nearly all obligations to the Empire, and Bohemia became, in effect, the Empire's most privileged kingdom - its king later an elector of emperors.
para2: Under the last Premyslids, Bohemia briefly dominated Central Europe: Ottokar II ruled from Prague to the Adriatic before falling in battle in 1278. The kingdom's golden age came under the Luxembourgs, above all Charles IV - king of Bohemia and Holy Roman Emperor - who made Prague the imperial capital, founded Charles University in 1348, rebuilt the royal castle of Hradcany and founded Prague's New Town, and made the Crown of Bohemia the Empire's richest land.
para3: Bohemia was also Europe's first Protestant battleground: from the teachings of Jan Hus - rector of Charles University from 1403, preaching the anti-papal doctrines of England's John Wycliffe - grew the Hussite movement (1402-1485), whose armies defeated four crusades sent by the Holy Roman Empire. A century before Luther, Bohemia had already defied Rome - and the Hussite movement is counted part of the roots of the Protestant Reformation.
para4: The kingdom passed to the Habsburgs in 1526 and remained theirs for nearly four centuries; after the Bohemian Revolt was suppressed, German gradually displaced Czech as the language of the Diet until the Czech National Revival of the 19th century. But the kingdom's name and crown survived until 1918, and Prague remained the heart of the Czech nation.

title: The Kingdom of England (Anglo-Saxon & Norman)
titleline: The Kingdom of England (Anglo-Saxon & Norman) - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of England (Anglo-Saxon and Norman). The Kingdom of England was born from the wreckage of the Viking invasions. In the 9th century the Danes overran every English kingdom but one: Alfred the Great of Wessex held out against them, retook London in 886, and styled himself King of the Anglo-Saxons. His son Edward the Elder and grandson Athelstan finished the work: in 927 Athelstan conquered the last Viking kingdom, York, and became the first king of all the English - the founder of a kingdom that would last, in one form, until 1707.
para2: Anglo-Saxon England was wealthy, administered, and cultivated - and fought over. Danish kings returned: in 1016 Cnut the Great made England part of his North Sea empire. But the decisive break came in 1066. When Edward the Confessor died childless, William, Duke of Normandy, claimed the crown, landed with his army, and killed King Harold at Hastings on 14 October 1066. On Christmas Day he was crowned King of England.
para3: The Norman Conquest was a revolution more total than almost any in European history. Within twenty years virtually all English land had passed to a few hundred Norman barons, held from the king by military service; castles rose everywhere; a French-speaking aristocracy ruled an English-speaking people; and the capital moved from Winchester to Westminster and London. Norman barons owed the king the service of their knights - the famous feudal levy of England - and the Conquest's castles, from the Tower of London outward, stamped the new order onto the landscape.
para4: Out of the fusion of conqueror and conquered came medieval England: its common law, its Parliament, and eventually the English language itself, reborn from the blending of Anglo-Saxon and French. Under Henry II (1154-1189), the first Angevin king, England became the heart of an Angevin realm with vast holdings in France - and the stage on which the struggles of crown, barons, and church would forge the institutions England still has.

title: The Kingdom of France (Capetians)
titleline: The Kingdom of France (Capetians) - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of France (Capetians). The Capetian dynasty ruled France from 987 - when the barons elected Hugh Capet to replace the last Carolingian - until 1328 in the direct line, and through its Valois and Bourbon branches until the Revolution: the longest royal line in European history. The first Capetians were among Europe's weakest kings, ruling directly little more than the Ile-de-France around Paris while great vassals like the dukes of Normandy and Aquitaine held more power than the crown.
para2: Two things saved them: an unbroken line of adult heirs for three hundred years (they crowned sons as co-kings in their own lifetimes), and the Church's loyalty. Then came the transformation. Philip II Augustus (1180-1223) broke the power of the English Plantagenet kings in France, seized their continental lands for the crown, and made the King of France the strongest ruler in the kingdom in fact as well as name. His grandson Louis VIII added Poitou and the south in the wake of the Albigensian Crusade.
para3: The dynasty's zenith was Louis IX - Saint Louis (1226-1270): the crusader king admired across Europe for his justice, who made the French crown the moral as well as political center of Christendom. Under his successors Philip III and Philip IV - who defied and kidnapped a pope, destroyed the Templars and seized their wealth in 1307, and summoned the first Estates General in 1302 - France stood as the pre-eminent power in Western Europe.
para4: When Philip IV's three sons all died without male heirs, the direct line ended in 1328 and the throne passed to the Valois - still Capetians by blood. The line Hugh founded has given France (and Navarre, Spain, Naples, and more) kings for a thousand years: a dynasty that turned a small lordship around Paris into the kingdom of France.

title: The Kingdom of Hungary
titleline: The Kingdom of Hungary - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Hungary. The Kingdom of Hungary was founded in 1000 and became one of medieval Europe's most durable states. It began when the Magyar grand prince Stephen was crowned king at Esztergom on Christmas Day 1000: St. Stephen and his Arpad dynasty, who led the monarchy for 300 years, made the once-raiding Magyars a settled Christian kingdom, and by the 12th century Hungary was a European power - from 1102 ruling Croatia in personal union as well.
para2: The kingdom nearly died in 1241-1242, when the Mongols devastated it, killing perhaps half its people; the Arpads rebuilt it with stone castles and invited settlers, and under Angevin and then native kings it flourished again. Its late-medieval zenith came under Matthias Corvinus (1458-1490), the Renaissance king whose library and Black Army made Buda one of the capitals of European culture - and who took Vienna itself.
para3: The catastrophe came on 29 August 1526 at the Battle of Mohacs, where the Ottoman army destroyed Hungarian power in an afternoon. The Habsburgs took the Hungarian throne - and held it until 1918 - while the country was partitioned into three parts: Habsburg Royal Hungary, Ottoman Hungary, and the semi-independent Principality of Transylvania. The heart of the old kingdom spent 150 years under Turkish rule, until Buda was recaptured in 1686.
para4: Hungary fought repeated wars of independence against the Habsburgs - in 1604-06, 1703-11, and 1848-49 - and from 1867 the Lands of the Crown of St. Stephen formed the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary. The monarchy collapsed in 1918, and the Treaty of Trianon in 1920 stripped the lands of the Holy Crown of two-thirds of their historic territory - a wound that defined Hungarian politics for a generation. Through it all, from 1000 onward, the Holy Crown of St. Stephen remained the symbol of the Hungarian state.

title: The Kingdom of Italy / Holy Roman Empire
titleline: The Kingdom of Italy / Holy Roman Empire - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Italy (Holy Roman Empire). The medieval Kingdom of Italy - 'Imperial Italy' - was the Italian third of the Holy Roman Empire: the lands north of the Papal States that emperors claimed as their own. It began in 951, when Otto I of Germany invaded Italy, married its widowed queen Adelaide, and took the Lombard crown at Pavia; in 962 he was crowned emperor in Rome, binding the crowns of Germany and Italy together for eight centuries.
para2: The union was always uneasy. The emperor was king of Italy, but he was usually an absentee, and Italy's real life went on in its cities. When emperors came south to make their power real - above all the Hohenstaufen Frederick Barbarossa - they met the Lombard League, an alliance of northern cities led by Milan that defeated Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176 and forced him to recognize their autonomy. The resulting wars between Guelphs (the anti-imperial party) and Ghibellines (the imperial party) - fought from 1216 to 1392 - defined Italian politics for most of two centuries.
para3: Imperial Italy's weakness was the city-states' opportunity: Milan, Venice's rivals like Genoa, Florence, and the communes of Lombardy grew rich and self-governing in the space between a distant emperor and a local pope. The Renaissance grew in precisely this gap.
para4: The kingdom lingered on paper into the modern age - emperors kept the title, and Imperial Italy's petty lords appealed to imperial courts until the end - until Napoleon dissolved the Holy Roman Empire itself. But its true legacy was negative and enormous: by preventing any single power from uniting medieval Italy, it left the peninsula what it had become after Legnano - a patchwork of autonomous cities and duchies only nominally tied to the Empire, a disunity that lasted into the 19th century.

title: The Kingdom of Poland
titleline: The Kingdom of Poland - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Poland. Poland entered history in 966, when Duke Mieszko I of the Polans accepted Christianity - a choice that anchored Poland to Latin Europe forever. His son Boleslaw the Brave was crowned the first King of Poland in 1025. The early kingdom was turbulent: a pagan reaction and foreign invasion shattered it in the 1030s, and though the crown was regained and lost again - Boleslaw II was exiled in 1079 for the murder of Bishop Stanislaus, Poland's national saint - Poland spent two centuries fragmented into duchies.
para2: Reunification came after failed attempts - Przemysl II was crowned in 1296 and murdered within months; Wenceslaus II of Bohemia wore the crown until 1305 - until Wladyslaw I the Elbow-High was crowned at the Wawel in Krakow in 1320. His son Casimir III the Great (1333-1370) - the only Polish king called 'the Great' - expanded into Red Ruthenia and transformed the kingdom's towns, administration, and army. When he died heirless on 5 November 1370, the Piast dynasty died with him.
para3: Casimir died heirless in 1370, and the crown passed to his Angevin nephew and then to his daughter Jadwiga, whose marriage in 1386 to Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania founded the Jagiellonian dynasty. For two centuries the Jagiellonians ruled not just Poland and Lithuania but, at times, Bohemia and Hungary too - the greatest dynastic bloc in Central Europe - while Poland's nobility built the parliamentary Sejm and, after the dynasty died out in 1572, the 'free election' of kings that would define the later Commonwealth.
para4: The medieval Kingdom of Poland survived, transformed, within the Commonwealth of Two Nations until the partitions destroyed it in 1795. But its medieval foundations - Catholic, Latin, Jagiellonian - are still the foundations of Poland today.

title: The Kingdom of Sicily
titleline: The Kingdom of Sicily - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Sicily. The Kingdom of Sicily (1130-1816) was medieval Europe's most remarkable melting pot: a kingdom where Norman, Greek, Arab, and Latin cultures fused under one crown. It was created by the Normans - descendants of Vikings, hired as mercenaries, who under Roger I conquered Sicily from its Muslim rulers (Palermo fell after a siege; the island was theirs by 1091) - when his son Roger II united the island, Malta, and the mainland south and was crowned king at Palermo on Christmas Day 1130, with the sanction of (anti)pope Anacletus II. His court, served by Greek, Saracen, and Latin scribes, was the most cosmopolitan court in Christendom - and the Curiae Generales he convened in 1130 has been called the first parliament in the modern sense.
para2: The kingdom passed by marriage to the Hohenstaufen emperors: Frederick II, half-Sicilian and raised in Palermo's cosmopolitan court, made the kingdom the center of his imperial world - until his line's defeat ended German rule and brought in Charles of Anjou's French armies.
para3: The turning point was 1282: the Sicilian Vespers, the great uprising that massacred the island's French Angevin rulers and handed Sicily over to the Crown of Aragon. The island and the mainland split - Sicily under Aragon, the mainland ('Naples') under Angevins and then Aragon too - and Sicily spent four centuries as a Mediterranean dependency: Aragonese, Spanish, briefly Savoyard and Austrian, and finally Bourbon.
para4: In 1816 the island and Naples merged into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, which lasted until Italian unification. But the Norman kingdom's imprint endures in Sicily's layered Greek-Arab-Norman identity - the memory of medieval Europe's most multicultural kingdom.

title: The Ostrogothic & Lombard Kingdoms
titleline: The Ostrogothic & Lombard Kingdoms - The History Web
para1: The Ostrogothic and Lombard Kingdoms. After the Western Roman Empire fell, Italy passed through two Germanic kingdoms. The first was the Ostrogothic (493-553): Theodoric the Great - who had spent his youth as a hostage in Constantinople and came to Italy with the Eastern emperor Zeno's commission - overthrew Odoacer, who had deposed the last Western emperor, and ruled from Ravenna for thirty-three years (493-526), preserving Roman administration under a Gothic warrior elite - a brief golden age of peace and order between two catastrophes.
para2: Theodoric's kingdom died with his dynasty: the emperor Justinian's armies invaded in 535, took Ravenna and captured the Gothic king Witiges - but the Goths rallied around Totila and reversed the conquest, and the war ground on for nearly twenty years. By the time the last Gothic king, Teia, fell at Mons Lactarius in 553, Italy was Byzantine - and ruined by a generation of sieges, sacks, and famine.
para3: The Lombards filled the vacuum almost at once: in 568 Alboin led his people over the Alps, and within a few years they held most of the peninsula, ruling from Pavia through semi-independent dukes. For two centuries the Lombard kingdom was Italy's dominant power, gradually Romanizing - Lombard speech, dress, and custom faded away - and converting from Arianism and paganism to Catholicism. But its duchies of Spoleto and Benevento stayed half-independent, and its wars with the popes proved fatal.
para4: When King Desiderius threatened Rome itself, the pope called in the Franks: in 774 Charlemagne took Pavia, sent Desiderius to a monastery, and crowned himself King of the Lombards. Italy's last Germanic kingdom ended - and Lombardy's very name is its memorial.

title: The Papal States
titleline: The Papal States - The History Web
para1: The Papal States. The Papal States were the popes' earthly kingdom: the band of territory across central Italy that the Bishop of Rome ruled as a sovereign prince for over eleven centuries (756-1870). They began with the 'Donation of Pepin' in 756, when the Frankish king Pepin, having defeated the Lombards, granted the pope the lands of central Italy - making the pope a territorial ruler and cementing the Frankish-papal alliance that would crown Charlemagne.
para2: A kingdom ruled by a churchman was a strange state, and its fortunes swung wildly. At its height, medieval popes were Europe's powerbrokers; at its low points the papacy was the plaything of Roman mobs, Roman barons, or foreign kings - most famously during the 'Babylonian Captivity' (1309-1376), when the popes abandoned Rome for Avignon under French influence. Renaissance popes like Alexander VI and Julius II - the 'Warrior Pope' who fought on his state's behalf - rebuilt papal power into one of Italy's principal secular lordships, though much of their territory long remained only nominally theirs, ruled by local princes.
para3: The states were always an anomaly: an elective theocracy with a flag, an army, and taxes. Italian nationalists saw them as the central obstacle to unification: by 1860 the Kingdom of Sardinia had taken most of them into the new Kingdom of Italy, and in 1870 Italian troops took Rome itself (20 September), leaving Pius IX holding only the Vatican - the self-styled 'prisoner in the Vatican.'
para4: For more than half a century the popes refused to recognize the loss, remaining self-styled 'prisoners in the Vatican' while Italy made Rome its capital - the 'Roman Question' that embittered church and state alike, still unresolved as the 1920s began.

title: The Reconquista
titleline: The Reconquista - The History Web
para1: The Reconquista. The Reconquista - the 'reconquest' of Spain from Muslim rule - was the longest war in European history: nearly 780 years from the first Christian victory at Covadonga (traditionally 718 or 722) to the fall of Granada in 1492. It began with a remnant: after Muslim armies destroyed the Visigothic kingdom in 711, survivors held out in the northern mountains of Asturias, and from that foothold the Christian kingdoms of Spain slowly grew.
para2: The advance came in waves. By the early 11th century the Caliphate of Cordoba had shattered into petty taifa states, which the northern kings raided and milked for tribute (parias). Toledo, the old Visigothic capital, fell permanently in 1085. Muslim Africa struck back twice - the Almoravids and then the Almohads - but the crusade of 1212 broke their power at Las Navas de Tolosa, and in a single generation the great cities fell: Cordoba in 1236, Valencia in 1238, Seville in 1248. Only Granada survived, as a tributary state, for 250 more years.
para3: The Reconquista was never a simple war of religions: Christian kings fought each other as readily as Muslims, Muslim taifas allied with Christian princes, and for centuries Christians, Muslims, and Jews lived mixed in the frontier society of convivencia. But as the frontier moved south, tolerance thinned.
para4: The end came on 2 January 1492, when the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella, received the surrender of the last Muslim ruler of Granada. Within months came the Alhambra Decree expelling Spain's Jews - some 200,000 people - and over the following century Spain's Muslims were forcibly converted and then expelled too. The Spain the Reconquista built was unified, militant, and intolerant - and, in the very year of Granada's fall, about to become a world empire.

title: The Republic of Genoa
titleline: The Republic of Genoa - The History Web
para1: The Republic of Genoa. The Republic of Genoa (1099-1797) was Venice's great rival: the smaller, scrappier maritime republic of the Ligurian coast, whose merchants and sailors contested the Mediterranean for three centuries. It rose with the Crusades: already in 1087 Genoese and Pisan fleets had struck North Africa and burned the Arab fleet at Mahdia, winning control of the western Mediterranean; Genoese ships then carried the First Crusade, blockading Antioch in 1098, and Genoese crossbowmen fought at the siege of Jerusalem in 1099 - and made its fortune where Venice was weak: the western Mediterranean and the Black Sea - Genoa held southern Crimea from 1266 to 1475, plus Corsica, Chios, and Lesbos.
para2: Genoa and Venice fought for supremacy for generations - the rivalry climaxed in the War of Chioggia (1378-1381): Genoa occupied the very lagoon of Venice but lost the war, and by the Treaty of Turin quit the contest for the East for good. Genoa turned west instead: to Spain, and to finance.
para3: For in the 16th century Genoa reinvented itself as the banker of Europe. Under Andrea Doria's constitution of 1528 and through the mighty Bank of Saint George (founded back in 1407), Genoese bankers became the long-lasting financial partners of the Spanish Empire, and the republic - its colonies gone - became one of the major financial centres of Europe.
para4: The republic declined with Spain, lingered through the 18th century - losing Corsica, its last great colony, in 1768 - and died in 1797 when Napoleon's armies turned it into the Ligurian Republic. Its legacy: the model of merchant finance that helped invent modern capitalism, and nearly seven centuries of proud Ligurian independence.

title: The Republic of Venice
titleline: The Republic of Venice - The History Web
para1: The Republic of Venice. The Republic of Venice - La Serenissima, 'the Most Serene' - was the longest-lived republic in history: eleven centuries (697-1797) under elected doges, from a huddle of lagoon refugees to the greatest commercial power of the Mediterranean. Born as a Byzantine outpost in the lagoons, Venice made the sea its walls and its road: its merchants monopolized the trade in spices, silk, and luxury between Europe and the East, and from 1109 its doges titled themselves lords of Dalmatia and Croatia as well as Venice.
para2: Venice's empire was a maritime one: the Dalmatian coast, Crete, Cyprus, and a chain of islands and ports across the eastern Mediterranean. Its defining moment came in 1204, when Venice diverted the Fourth Crusade to sack Constantinople - the greatest Christian city on earth - and took as its share the title 'Lord of a quarter and a half of the Eastern Roman Empire,' with Crete, ports in the Morea, and islands across the Aegean - the maritime empire Venice called the Stato da Mar.
para3: The republic was an oligarchy of merchant families, but a stable one: the Serrata of 1297 locked power into the Great Council's families, and the dreaded Council of Ten, created after the Tiepolo conspiracy of 1310, repressed any threat to the state - including Doge Marino Faliero himself, executed for his own coup in 1355. Venice saw off its greatest rival in the War of Chioggia (1378-1381), after which Genoa quit the contest for Mediterranean supremacy.
para4: Decline was long and graceful: the Portuguese route around Africa and the rise of the Ottomans slowly strangled its trade. The end came in 1797, when Napoleon simply abolished the ancient republic and handed it to Austria by the Treaty of Campo Formio. But Venice remains what it always was: a city like no other, built on water by merchants who ruled an empire of the sea.

title: The Serbian Empire
titleline: The Serbian Empire - The History Web
para1: The Serbian Empire. The Serbian Empire was Serbia's moment as the master of the Balkans - brief, brilliant, and fatal. It grew from the medieval Serbian kingdom, but it was Stefan Dusan 'the Mighty' who seized the chance offered by Byzantine weakness: from 1333 he conquered Ohrid, Prilep, and Kastoria, then Thessaly, Albania, Epirus, and most of Macedonia - not in field battles but by besieging cities. By 1345 he ruled half the Balkans, more than the Byzantine or Bulgarian empires, and proclaimed himself Tsar at Serres; on 16 April 1346 he was crowned 'Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks' at Skopje by the newly elevated Serbian patriarch, in a claim to succeed Byzantium itself.
para2: At its height Dusan's empire stretched from the Danube to the Gulf of Corinth - the most powerful state in Southeast Europe, multi-ethnic and multi-lingual, with Kosovo as its political and religious heart. Dusan ruled it through his Code of 1349, one of the great law codes of the medieval Slavic world, blending Byzantine, customary, and Serbian law.
para3: The empire died with its maker. Dusan died suddenly in 1355, and under his son Uros 'the Weak' the great lords tore the empire apart; it effectively ended by 1371. From its ruins, Moravian Serbia emerged as the largest Serbian state under the Lazarevic dynasty - until it met the Ottomans at the legendary Battle of Kosovo in 1389, the battle that became the founding myth of Serbian nationhood.
para4: Serbia spent centuries under Ottoman rule. But Dusan's empire and Kosovo's memory - patriarchate, code, and battle - kept the idea of Serbia alive and drove its rebirth in the 19th century: the dream of the Balkan empire that lasted one man's lifetime.

title: The Swiss Confederacy
titleline: The Swiss Confederacy - The History Web
para1: The Swiss Confederacy. The Swiss Confederacy began as an oath in the mountains: on 1 August 1291, three Alpine valley communities - Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden - swore an 'Everlasting League' of mutual defense. They were reichsfrei - answerable to no lord but the emperor himself - and when the Habsburgs tried to turn that theoretical overlordship into real rule, the forest cantons fought.
para2: The Swiss proved that valley communities could beat knights: at Morgarten (1315) they destroyed Duke Leopold I's Habsburg army, and at Sempach (1386) they killed Leopold III and shattered another, and at Nafels (1388) they won again. They also saw off the Guglers - marauding mercenary knights from France - in 1375. Canton by canton the league grew - Lucerne, Zurich, Bern, and five more joined the original three - bound by a web of pacts like the Sempacherbrief of 1393, in which all eight cantons promised that none would make war without the consent of all.
para3: The 15th century made them a power: they shattered Charles the Bold of Burgundy in the Burgundian Wars (1470s), and in 1499 victory over Emperor Maximilian I in the Swabian War secured de facto independence from the Holy Roman Empire - a confederation of thirteen cantons that also took the Ticino during the Italian Wars, governed by periodic diets, without king, capital, or common government: an anomaly in a Europe of monarchies.
para4: The confederacy had no king, no capital, and no common government - only periodic diets and sworn pacts - an anomaly in a Europe of monarchies, and the direct ancestor of the modern Swiss federal state, which still celebrates the oath of 1 August 1291 as its national day.

title: The Visigothic Kingdom
titleline: The Visigothic Kingdom - The History Web
para1: The Visigothic Kingdom. The Visigothic Kingdom (418-711) was the successor state Rome made in Spain - and one of the most remarkable of the Germanic kingdoms that rose from the Western Empire's fall. The Visigoths had entered history violently, sacking Rome itself under Alaric in 410; eight years later, as Roman allies, they settled in Gaul with a capital at Toulouse, and from there spread into Spain, which they made their true home.
para2: The kingdom had two lives. From Toulouse the Visigoths ruled southern Gaul and most of Spain until 507, when Clovis and the Franks crushed them at Vouille and drove them south of the Pyrenees. From its new capital at Toledo, the kingdom then became genuinely Spanish - and the most Romanized of all the successor states. Its greatest moment came under Reccared: in 589 he renounced the Arian Christianity of the Gothic elite for the Catholic faith of his Hispano-Roman subjects, uniting the two peoples of his kingdom in one church.
para3: Visigothic Spain was learned and legislated: its kings issued law codes for Goths and Romans alike, and Toledo hosted church councils that shaped Spanish Christianity for centuries. But the monarchy was elective and bloody - noble factions murdered kings and fought civil wars over the succession, weakening the state at its core.
para4: The end came with terrifying speed: in 711 a Muslim army crossed from North Africa, defeated and killed King Roderic at the Guadalete, and within a few years almost the whole peninsula was under Muslim rule. The three-hundred-year kingdom vanished almost overnight - but its survivors in the northern mountains kept the name and the memory alive, and from them grew the Christian kingdoms of the Reconquista.

title: The Goths and the Alans
titleline: The Goths and the Alans - The History Web
para1: The Goths were Germanic peoples who, by the 3rd century CE, had moved from the Baltic region to the lands north of the Black Sea, where they split into two broad groups: the Greuthungi, later called Ostrogoths, and the Tervingi, later called Visigoths. From the Pontic steppe they raided the Roman Balkans and Asia Minor by land and sea, defeating and killing the emperor Decius at Abritus in 251. Contact with Rome also transformed them: Gothic mercenaries served in Roman armies, Gothic captives and traders adopted Roman goods, and the missionary Ulfilas converted many Goths to the homoean (Arian) form of Christianity, devising a Gothic alphabet to translate the Bible.
para2: The Alans were an Iranian-speaking nomadic people of the steppe between the Don and the Caspian, famous as horsemen and heavy cavalry. Pressured and partly subdued by the Huns in the 370s, some Alans joined the Hunnic empire while others fled west. In 406 a large body of Alans crossed the Rhine alongside the Vandals and Suebi, fought their way through Gaul, and passed into Spain in 409. There the Vandal-Alan bloc divided the peninsula, until Visigothic attacks on behalf of Rome shattered the Alans as an independent power around 418. The surviving Alans of Spain put themselves under the Vandal king Gunderic and crossed with the Vandals to Africa in 429, where 'rex Vandalorum et Alanorum', king of the Vandals and Alans, remained the royal title of the Carthage kingdom.
para3: The Visigoths made their own deal with Rome after sacking it in 410: settled first in Aquitaine as federate soldiers, they built a kingdom centered on Toulouse, fought Attila's Huns beside the Romans at the Catalaunian Fields in 451, and under Euric (466-484) ruled most of Spain and southern Gaul. Defeated by the Franks at Vouille in 507, they kept their Spanish kingdom, based on Toledo, until it fell to Muslim armies in 711. The Ostrogoths, after years in the Balkans, invaded Italy in 489 under Theodoric, who overthrew Odoacer and ruled a Romano-Gothic state from Ravenna, preserving Roman administration, law and letters under figures such as Boethius and Cassiodorus.
para4: Justinian's wars destroyed the Ostrogothic kingdom in a ruinous twenty-year struggle (535-554) that left Italy devastated for the Lombards who followed. The Visigothic kingdom of Toledo lasted longer, converted from Arian to Catholic Christianity under Reccared in 589, and developed a distinctive Hispano-Gothic law and church culture before its sudden collapse in 711. Alans remaining in the Caucasus survived as the medieval Alania, ancestors of the modern Ossetians, while Alan groups in Gaul left place-names such as Alencon. Together, Goths and Alans show how the peoples of the migration age could shatter Roman provinces and yet also preserve and reshape Roman civilization.

title: The Saxons, Angles and Jutes
titleline: The Saxons, Angles and Jutes - The History Web
para1: The Saxons, Angles and Jutes were Germanic peoples of the North Sea coastlands, Saxons from the lower Elbe region, Angles from the Schleswig-Angeln peninsula, and Jutes, probably, from Jutland, who migrated to Britain in the 5th and 6th centuries CE. After Rome withdrew its legions around 410, the Romano-British civitates faced Pictish and Irish raiding. According to the tradition preserved by Bede, the British king Vortigern hired Saxon mercenaries led by the brothers Hengist and Horsa, who then turned on their employers and invited more settlers across the sea. Archaeology confirms a deep cultural shift: new styles of pottery, dress fasteners, houses and cremation and inhumation cemeteries spread across eastern and southern England in the 5th century.
para2: Settlement proceeded by small groups of warriors, farmers and families rather than by coordinated conquest, and British resistance was real. The Britons won a major victory at Mons Badonicus (Mount Badon) around 500, associated in later legend with King Arthur, which checked the invaders for a generation. But the balance tipped decisively in the later 6th century, as Anglian and Saxon warbands carved out permanent kingdoms. In the process much of the Romano-British urban, Christian and Latin-speaking order vanished from what became England, though British communities and British Christianity survived strongly in Wales, Cornwall and the north.
para3: By about 600 the settlers had formed a patchwork of kingdoms traditionally called the Heptarchy: Kent, linked to the Jutes and famous for its early law code; the Saxon kingdoms of Sussex, Wessex and Essex; the Anglian kingdoms of East Anglia, Mercia and Northumbria; and smaller peoples such as the Hwicce and the Middle Angles. These kingdoms fought constantly for overlordship, and their kings traced descent from Woden. Pagan cemeteries such as Sutton Hoo, whose great ship burial of about 625 held a king's helmet, sword, and gold-and-garnet regalia, reveal an aristocratic warrior culture tied by gift-giving and feasting, celebrated in the Old English epic Beowulf.
para4: The conversion of the English began when Pope Gregory the Great sent Augustine to Kent in 597; King Aethelberht, whose wife was a Frankish Christian princess, allowed the mission to preach, and Canterbury became the English church's center. Irish monks from Iona converted Northumbria from the 630s, and the Synod of Whitby (664) aligned the English kingdoms on Roman practice. Christianity brought literacy back, and with it charters, written law codes and eventually the monastic scholarship of Bede's Northumbria. The Angles and Saxons gave England its name ('land of the Angles'), its language, and the kingdoms from which a united English monarchy would later emerge.

title: The Avar Khaganate
titleline: The Avar Khaganate - The History Web
para1: The Avar Khaganate (567-822) was a steppe empire in Central Europe created by the Avars, a nomadic people who appeared on Rome's Danube frontier in 558, fleeing the expansion of the Turks in Central Asia. Byzantine diplomats employed them as allies and mercenaries, but the Avars soon moved west, and in 567, allied with the Lombards, they destroyed the Gepid kingdom; when the Lombards departed for Italy in 568, the Avars took over the whole Carpathian Basin. From the Hungarian plain, rich grazing for their herds, the khagans ruled a multi-ethnic empire of Slavic, Germanic and Romance-speaking subjects stretching from the Alps to the Black Sea.
para2: Under their long-ruling khagan Bayan I, the Avars fought the Byzantine Empire for control of the Balkans. They captured the fortress of Sirmium in 582 after a long blockade, raided deep into Thrace and Greece, and pushed Slavic settlers ahead of their armies into imperial lands. Tribute extracted from Constantinople funded a court famous for goldwork, and Avar archaeology is rich in gold and silver belt fittings, weapons and jewelry showing steppe, Byzantine and Persian influences. Avar power also reorganized the peoples of the north: the first Slavic 'kingdom' of Samo (c. 623-658) was born from a revolt against Avar overlords, and the Bulgars on the lower Danube slipped from Avar control in the 630s.
para3: The khaganate's greatest bid came in 626, when the Avars, allied with the Persian Empire, besieged Constantinople itself. The failure of the assault, broken by the city's walls and fleet, damaged the khagan's prestige across the steppe, and subject peoples began to defect. Civil war among rival Avar factions followed in the 630s, and the empire settled into a smaller but still formidable power centered on the fortified 'ring' encampments of the Hungarian plain, exacting tribute and service from the Slavs of the Carpathians.
para4: The end came from the west. Charlemagne's Franks, allied with dissident Avars and Bulgars, smashed the khaganate in campaigns between 791 and 796, storming the great ring and carrying off its accumulated treasure, which, contemporaries said, enriched the Frankish kingdom for years. Avar power collapsed so completely that a later proverb asked, 'where are the Avars now?', and by 822 the last khagan had accepted Frankish overlordship and baptism before disappearing from history. The khaganate left no written language of its own, but it reshaped eastern Europe: it accelerated Slavic settlement across the Balkans and central Europe and left a legacy of horse gear, warfare and goldsmithing adopted by its successor peoples.

title: The Vandal Kingdom
titleline: The Vandal Kingdom - The History Web
para1: The Vandal Kingdom (439-534) was a Germanic kingdom established in Roman North Africa by the Vandals and Alans, peoples who had crossed the Rhine in 406, fought their way through Gaul, and settled in Spain in 409. Pressed by the Visigoths acting for Rome, some eighty thousand Vandals and Alans crossed the Strait of Gibraltar into Mauretania in 429 under their new king Genseric, one of the most capable war leaders of the age. Marching east along the coast, defeating Roman and Moorish forces alike, Genseric took Hippo Regius in 431, shortly after the death of its bishop Augustine, and in 439 captured Carthage, the second city of the western Mediterranean.
para2: From Carthage the Vandals did something no other successor people managed: they built a fleet. Vandal squadrons seized the Balearic Islands, Sardinia and Corsica, raided the coasts of Italy and Greece, and in 455, after the murder of the emperor Valentinian III, Genseric landed in Italy and sacked Rome itself, carrying off the empress Eudoxia and her daughters and treasure that included the Temple vessels Titus had taken from Jerusalem. Roman attempts to crush the kingdom ended in disaster: the great joint expedition of 468, assembled by both halves of the empire under Basiliscus, was destroyed off Cape Bon by Vandal fireships. The Eastern Empire made peace in 474, recognizing Vandal control of Africa and the islands.
para3: The kingdom was a thin military elite ruling over a large Roman population. The Vandals were homoean (Arian) Christians, while their Roman subjects were overwhelmingly Catholic; Genseric and his son Huneric exiled bishops and clergy and confiscated Catholic churches, though persecution eased under later kings. Roman administration, taxation and coinage continued, the elite of Carthage kept much of its culture, and the countryside remained prosperous through its olive oil and grain exports. But the dynasty was unstable: Genseric's will enforced succession by the eldest male of the family, producing a string of aging kings and palace coups, and Moorish confederations pressed the kingdom's borders.
para4: In 530 the pro-Roman king Hilderic was overthrown by his cousin Gelimer, giving the eastern emperor Justinian a pretext to intervene. In 533 the general Belisarius landed with about fifteen thousand men, defeated Gelimer at Ad Decimum, took Carthage, and destroyed Vandal resistance at Tricamarum; Gelimer surrendered in 534 and ended his days on an estate in Galatia. North Africa became a Byzantine province, the Vandal aristocracy was shipped east or absorbed, and the Vandals vanished as a people so completely that their name survived mainly as a synonym for destruction, a verdict of the Roman writers whose churches and cities they had taken.

title: The Vikings
titleline: The Vikings - The History Web
para1: The Vikings were seafaring Scandinavians, Norwegians, Danes and Swedes, whose raids and settlements reshaped northern Europe between about 793 and 1066. Their era opens dramatically with the raid on the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793, recorded with horror by English churchmen. Behind the expansion lay growing populations, quarrels among petty kings, the lure of portable wealth in monasteries and towns, and above all the Viking ship: a clinker-built, shallow-draft vessel with sail and oars that could cross open seas yet slip up rivers, letting raiders strike far inland without warning. 'Viking' was an activity, going raiding and trading overseas, as much as a people.
para2: Norwegian Vikings sailed west, settling the Faroes, Shetland, Orkney, the Hebrides and much of coastal Ireland, where they founded Dublin. From there they pushed to Iceland in the 870s, which became a self-governing commonwealth of farmers with an open-air assembly, the Althing, and then to Greenland under Erik the Red around 985. Leif Erikson reached North America about the year 1000, and the settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland proves a Norse presence five centuries before Columbus. Danes concentrated on England and Francia: the Great Heathen Army of 865 conquered most of Anglo-Saxon England before Alfred of Wessex stopped it at Edington in 878, leaving the Danelaw under Norse rule, while other Danes besieged Paris in 845 and 885 and won the Seine valley that became Normandy in 911.
para3: Swedish Vikings went east, down the rivers of what is now Russia and Ukraine. Known there as the Rus', they traded furs, slaves, wax and amber to the Black and Caspian Seas, founded river towns such as Novgorod, and according to the Primary Chronicle were invited to rule: the Varangian Rurik's dynasty ended up at Kiev, whose princes grew rich on the route 'from the Varangians to the Greeks'. Swedes served as the Byzantine emperor's Varangian Guard, raided the Caspian coasts of Persia, and left runic graffiti as far away as Hagia Sophia. Viking-age Scandinavia itself was transformed, as the kings of Denmark, Norway and Sweden converted to Christianity and forged national monarchies around the year 1000, and the Danish king Cnut briefly ruled an empire of England, Denmark and Norway (1016-1035).
para4: The Viking Age closed with the failed Norwegian invasion of England defeated at Stamford Bridge in 1066, days before the Norman Conquest, and with the growing strength of European states that could resist raiders. Its legacy runs deep: Icelandic sagas preserving a unique window on Norse society; law, ship technology and trade networks from Dublin to Kiev; the ancestry of Normandy's dukes, Russia's first dynasty and many English families; and the Old Norse words embedded in English. Far from being only raiders, the Vikings were also farmers, merchants, explorers and state-builders whose diaspora connected the Atlantic islands to the rivers of the east.

title: The Duchy of Normandy
titleline: The Duchy of Normandy - The History Web
para1: The Duchy of Normandy (911-1204) began with a bargain between the West Frankish king Charles the Simple and the Viking leader Rollo at the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte in 911: Rollo received lands around Rouen on the lower Seine, accepted baptism, and pledged to defend the kingdom against other Vikings. Within a century the Norse settlers, 'Northmen', had absorbed the local Frankish population, adopting its language, religion and law while keeping a reputation for seamanship and war. Under dukes such as Richard I 'the Fearless' and Richard II 'the Good', Normandy became one of the best-organized principalities in France, its dukes controlling castles, mints and a loyal mounted warrior class, and patronizing monasteries such as Fecamp, Jumieges and Mont-Saint-Michel.
para2: Norman energies overflowed the duchy's borders. In the 11th century Norman knights seeking fortune went to southern Italy, where they seized Apulia, Calabria and Sicily from Byzantine and Muslim rulers, and to the edges of Spain and the crusading East. At home, Duke William, the illegitimate but forceful son of Robert I, survived a dangerous minority and the battle of Val-es-Dunes (1047) to impose his authority. Marrying Matilda of Flanders and cultivating papal support, he transformed Normandy into a springboard for the most consequential gamble of the century.
para3: In 1066 William claimed the English throne after the death of Edward the Confessor, arguing that Edward had promised it to him and that Harold Godwinson had sworn to support him. He assembled a fleet and an army drawn from across northern France, landed in Sussex, and defeated and killed Harold at Hastings on 14 October 1066. The Norman Conquest replaced England's ruling class wholesale: Norman French became the language of court and law, castles rose across the country, the Domesday Book of 1086 surveyed the conquered land in unprecedented detail, and the English church was reorganized under Norman bishops. Normandy and England were now held in personal union, binding English politics to northern France for a hundred and fifty years.
para4: The union was often uneasy: William's sons fought over the inheritance, and after Henry I's son died in the White Ship disaster of 1120, civil war followed under Stephen. Henry II Plantagenet, son of Geoffrey of Anjou and Henry I's daughter Matilda, inherited Normandy with England in 1154 and built the Angevin 'empire'. Normandy's independent life ended in 1204, when King Philip Augustus of France conquered the duchy from King John, driving a wedge between England and France that fed centuries of conflict. The Normans' legacy is immense: England's monarchy, law and language all bear their stamp, and Norman churches and castles from Durham to Sicily still mark the lands they ruled.

title: The Angevin Empire
titleline: The Angevin Empire - The History Web
para1: The Angevin Empire (1154-1214) is the name historians give to the collection of lands ruled by the first Plantagenet king, Henry II, and his sons. Its core was the county of Anjou, whose counts built power by war and marriage; Geoffrey Plantagenet of Anjou married Matilda, daughter of Henry I of England, and their son Henry inherited England in 1154 after the civil wars of Stephen's reign. To England, Normandy and Anjou, Henry added by marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine the vast duchy of Aquitaine stretching to the Pyrenees, and overlordship over Brittany, Wales, Scotland and, later, much of Ireland. At its height this 'empire' controlled half of France and the whole of England, making Henry richer in land than his nominal overlord, the king of France.
para2: The empire was a patchwork, not a state: each land kept its own law, coinage, language and institutions, and the king ruled by constant travel between them, from Newcastle to the Pyrenees. Henry II's great work was administrative. In England he developed royal justice, itinerant judges, juries of presentment and the writ system that became the common law, and he reformed finances after the anarchy. His attempt to extend royal jurisdiction over the church led to his famous quarrel with Archbishop Thomas Becket, whose murder in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170, by knights taking the king's angry words literally, shocked Christendom and forced Henry to compromise and do penance.
para3: Henry's empire was also a family firm that turned on itself. Eleanor and her sons resented his control, and in 1173-1174 the Young King Henry, Richard and Geoffrey, backed by the kings of France and Scotland, rose in a great rebellion that Henry defeated. Imprisoned for fifteen years, Eleanor outlived the struggle; the Young King and Geoffrey died rebelling. Richard I 'the Lionheart', king from 1189, spent barely six months of his reign in England: he led the Third Crusade to victory at Arsuf and the walls of Jerusalem, was captured on his way home and ransomed for a crippling sum, then died campaigning in France in 1199, leaving the inheritance to his brother John.
para4: John's reign undid the empire. Philip II of France, a patient and ruthless rival, used John's feudal failures, his quarrel with the Lusignans, and the mysterious death of his nephew Arthur of Brittany to declare his French lands forfeit, then conquered Normandy in 1204 and Anjou, Maine and Touraine soon after. John's attempt to win them back ended with his allies' crushing defeat at Bouvines in 1214, and his overtaxed English barons forced Magna Carta on him in 1215. What remained to the Plantagenets was England and Gascony, and a lasting French-English enmity. The Angevin experiment still mattered: England's common law and administration were forged in it, and the dream of recovering the lost lands helped drive the Hundred Years' War.

title: The Hundred Years' War
titleline: The Hundred Years' War - The History Web
para1: The Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) was a series of conflicts between the kings of England and France over the French crown and the English-held lands in France. Its roots lay in the odd position of English kings, who ruled Gascony as vassals of the French crown, and in the succession crisis of 1328, when the direct Capetian line failed. Edward III of England, whose mother was the last Capetian king's sister, was passed over for Philip VI of Valois; after years of friction over Gascony and Flanders, Edward claimed the French crown in 1340, quartering the lilies of France with the leopards of England on his arms.
para2: The first phase favored England spectacularly. English armies, built around dismounted men-at-arms and longbowmen, won at Crecy in 1346 and captured Calais after a famous siege; at Poitiers in 1356 the Black Prince captured King John II of France himself, who died in captivity awaiting a ruinous ransom. The Treaty of Bretigny (1360) gave Edward an enlarged Aquitaine in full sovereignty, but it unraveled within a decade as Charles V of France and his constable Bertrand du Guesclin recovered nearly everything by patient attrition. Both crowns were meanwhile strained by taxation, plague and revolt: the Jacquerie in France and the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 in England.
para3: War resumed under Henry V of England, who exploited a French civil war between Burgundians and Armagnacs. His victory at Agincourt in 1415, where longbowmen annihilated the flower of French chivalry, led to the conquest of Normandy and the Treaty of Troyes (1420), by which Henry married Charles VI's daughter and was recognized as heir to France. Both kings died in 1422, leaving the infant Henry VI as nominal king of both realms. The turning point came in 1429, when Joan of Arc, a peasant girl convinced she was sent by God, rallied the Dauphin Charles' cause, relieved the siege of Orleans and saw him crowned at Reims as Charles VII. Captured by the Burgundians and sold to the English, she was tried and burned in 1431, but the French recovery she began did not stop.
para4: The Burgundians abandoned the English alliance at Arras in 1435, Paris was retaken in 1436, and Charles VII reformed his army with permanent companies and a powerful train of artillery. Normandy fell after the battle of Formigny in 1450, and Gascony after Castillon in 1453, where French cannon decided the day; England kept only Calais, until 1558. The war transformed both kingdoms: France emerged with a standing army, direct royal taxation and a stronger monarchy, while England, bankrupted and demoralized, slid toward the Wars of the Roses. It also changed warfare, ending the dominance of feudal cavalry, and forged new senses of English and French national identity, symbolized above all by Joan of Arc.
