title: The Investiture Controversy
titleline: The Investiture Controversy - The History Web
para1: The Investiture Controversy (1075-1122) was the great medieval struggle between popes and kings over who should appoint bishops and abbots, the men who held both spiritual authority and vast lands and political power. Bishops were essential officers of royal government, and kings had long 'invested' them with their offices, sometimes for a fee, a practice reformers condemned as simony. In the 11th century a reform movement centered on the papacy, above all Pope Gregory VII (reigned 1073-1085), set out to free the church from lay control. In 1075 Gregory prohibited lay investiture outright, claiming that spiritual office could come only from the church, and that the pope stood above kings.
para2: The claim collided head-on with Henry IV of Germany, who depended on appointing loyal bishops to rule his far-flung lands. After Henry ignored the ban and backed rival bishops at the Synod of Worms (1076), Gregory excommunicated and deposed him, releasing his subjects from obedience. With German princes threatening to elect a new king, Henry made his famous winter journey across the Alps to Canossa in January 1077, where, according to tradition, he stood three days barefoot in the snow before the pope absolved him. The drama settled nothing: civil war continued in Germany, Henry appointed an antipope, and in 1084 he took Rome itself. Gregory was rescued by his Norman allies and died in exile at Salerno in 1085, saying, 'I have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore I die in exile.'
para3: The struggle widened beyond Germany. In England, Archbishop Anselm of Canterbury quarreled with Kings William II and Henry I over investiture and appeals to Rome; France kept a looser, more workable practice of royal influence over elections; and the Norman rulers of southern Italy backed the reform popes as a counterweight to the German emperors. Under Urban II the conflict temporarily took second place to the First Crusade, but the underlying question, where the church's authority ended and the state's began, remained contested across Europe.
para4: Exhaustion produced compromise in the Concordat of Worms (1122) between Pope Calixtus II and Emperor Henry V. The emperor renounced investiture with ring and staff, the spiritual symbols, and guaranteed free elections, while in Germany he retained the right to be present at elections and to invest bishops with their temporal lands by the scepter. In practice, kings kept great influence and popes kept the principle of spiritual independence. The controversy had lasting effects: it defined the medieval distinction between spiritual and temporal power, strengthened the papal monarchy that dominated the 12th and 13th centuries, weakened imperial control in Germany and Italy, and set the template for church-state argument in Europe for centuries.

title: The Hanseatic League
titleline: The Hanseatic League - The History Web
para1: The Hanseatic League (c. 1150-1669) was a confederation of merchant guilds and trading towns that dominated commerce in the Baltic and North Seas for four centuries. It grew from partnerships among German merchants trading to Gotland and England, and took institutional shape after Lubeck, founded in 1158, became the hub of the Baltic trade in herring, salt, furs, grain, timber, wax and metals. Towns joined for protection of their merchants abroad and privileges at home; at its height the league counted around two hundred member and associated towns, from Novgorod in the east to London and Bruges in the west, though it had no permanent government, treasury or army.
para2: The league's power rested on its kontore, fortified trading compounds in foreign ports. The four great kontore were Novgorod, where Germans bought Russian furs and wax; Bergen, which funneled Norwegian dried cod to Europe; Bruges, the financial market of the west; and the London Steelyard. Hanseatic privileges were won by negotiation and by economic pressure: a boycott could starve a prince of revenue, and a blockade could ruin a port. When Waldemar IV of Denmark tried to break Hanseatic dominance of the herring fisheries, the league went to war and forced the Treaty of Stralsund (1370), which confirmed its control of Danish trade and even a say in the Danish succession, the peak of its political power.
para3: Hanseatic ships, above all the broad, high-sided cog, sailed regular routes carrying bulk goods that fed and clothed northern Europe: Baltic grain to the Low Countries, salt from Luneburg to the fisheries, English wool to Flemish looms, and Russian furs and flax to the west. The league enforced common rules of trade, standardized weights, and protected its members with convoys and reciprocal justice. It also shaped its cities: the brick-Gothic town halls, churches and merchants' houses of Lubeck, Stralsund, Wismar, Danzig (Gdansk), Riga and Tallinn, and the legal self-government of towns under 'Lubeck law', spread the same civic culture around the Baltic rim.
para4: From the 15th century the league slowly lost ground. The herring shoals left the Baltic sounds, Dutch and English merchants outcompeted the cogs with cheaper shipping, the kontore in Novgorod (1494) and London (1598) were closed, and rising territorial states, Sweden, Denmark, Brandenburg and the Polish kings, no longer tolerated an independent power. The Thirty Years' War shattered the Baltic economy, and the last Hanseatic diet met in 1669 with only nine towns attending; Lubeck, Hamburg and Bremen kept the 'Hanseatic' title long after. The league's real legacy is the urban, trading culture of northern Europe: it tied the Baltic world into the European economy and showed how cities, organized together, could rival kings.

title: The Teutonic Knights and the Baltic Crusades
titleline: The Teutonic Knights and the Baltic Crusades - The History Web
para1: The Teutonic Order (founded 1190) was a German military religious order born during the Third Crusade, when merchants from Bremen and Lubeck set up a field hospital outside Acre. Modeled on the Templars and Hospitallers, it combined monastic vows with warfare, and after the failure of the crusades in the Holy Land it found a new field in Europe. In 1211 the order campaigned in Transylvania against the Cumans, and in 1226 Duke Conrad of Masovia invited it to fight the pagan Prussians on his Baltic frontier. Backed by imperial and papal grants, the knights began a conquest that lasted fifty years, building castles, founding towns and settling German colonists.
para2: The Prussian Crusade was part of the wider Baltic Crusades (12th-14th centuries), church-blessed campaigns against the pagan peoples of the southern and eastern Baltic coast: Wends, Prussians, Lithuanians, Latvians and Estonians. The Sword Brothers, founded in Riga in 1202, conquered Livonia before being destroyed by Lithuanians at Saule in 1236 and merged into the Teutonic Order as its Livonian branch. The Danes took northern Estonia. Alongside conquest came conversion, colonization and the founding of cities, Riga, Danzig, Konigsberg, Thorn, under German town law, and by 1300 the southeastern Baltic was tied into Latin Christendom and Hanseatic trade.
para3: From its new capital at Marienburg (1309) the order ruled a unique state: a theocracy of knight-brothers and priests governing Prussian, Polish and German subjects through castle districts. Its wars continued against still-pagan Lithuania and increasingly against Christian Poland, which disputed Pomerelia, seized by the order in 1308. The turning point came in 1410 at Grunwald (Tannenberg), where the Polish-Lithuanian army of Wladyslaw Jagiello and Vytautas destroyed the order's field army and killed its grand master. The order survived the siege of Marienburg, but the enormous indemnity of 1411 and the costs of war ruined its finances and discredited its mission now that Lithuania was Christian.
para4: In 1454 the order's own Prussian subjects, the German and Polish towns and nobles of the Prussian Confederation, revolted with Polish support. After the Thirteen Years' War the Peace of Thorn (1466) split the state: western 'Royal Prussia' went to Poland, while the order kept East Prussia as a Polish vassal. In 1525 Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg converted to Lutheranism and secularized the remnant as the Duchy of Prussia, a fief of the Polish crown, the seed of the later Prussian state. The order's legacy is double: it brought towns, castles, churches and German settlement to the Baltic, and it left a long memory of conquest in Polish and Lithuanian national history.

title: The Kalmar Union
titleline: The Kalmar Union - The History Web
para1: The Kalmar Union (1397-1523) joined the three Scandinavian kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden under a single crown. Its architect was Margaret I, daughter of the Danish king Valdemar IV and wife of King Haakon VI of Norway. After the deaths of her husband (1380) and her son Olaf (1387), Margaret was accepted as regent of Denmark and Norway, then defeated and captured Albert of Mecklenburg, the unpopular German king of Sweden, in 1389. In 1397 at Kalmar her grandnephew Erik of Pomerania was crowned king of all three realms, while Margaret continued to rule in fact until her death in 1412.
para2: The union was personal, not a merger: each kingdom kept its own laws, councils and administration. Margaret governed skillfully, recovering crown lands, balancing the powerful nobles and churchmen of three countries, and maintaining peace with the Hanseatic League, which dominated Baltic trade. Denmark was the senior partner, supplying most kings and the union's foreign policy; Sweden, the largest and poorest realm, chafed at Danish officials and taxes. Norwegian and Swedish councils hoped the union would protect them from German princes and the Hansa, but resentment grew whenever royal power reached too far into local affairs.
para3: Erik of Pomerania's autocratic rule and his wars with the counts of Holstein and the Hansa strained the union to breaking. Sweden rose under the peasant-noble revolt of Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson (1434-1436), and Erik was deposed in all three kingdoms (1439-1442), replaced by his nephew Christopher and then, in Sweden and Norway, by Karl Knutsson (Bonde). For the rest of the 15th century the union existed on and off: Danish kings of the Oldenburg dynasty, from Christian I (1448), were repeatedly recognized in Sweden and repeatedly expelled by Swedish regents such as Sten Sture, who defeated Christian I at Brunkeberg in 1471.
para4: Christian II briefly restored the union by force, but his massacre of Swedish nobles and churchmen at the 'Stockholm Bloodbath' (1520) provoked the final break: Gustav Vasa's rebellion drove the Danes out, and in 1523 Gustav was elected king of an independent Sweden. Denmark-Norway remained united until 1814. The Kalmar Union showed both the pull of Scandinavian cooperation and the strength of separate national institutions; its failure left Denmark and Sweden as rivals who fought for Baltic mastery for the next three centuries.

title: The Kingdom of Scotland
titleline: The Kingdom of Scotland - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Scotland (c. 843-1707) grew from the union of the Picts and the Scots of Dal Riata under Kenneth MacAlpin, traditionally dated to 843. The early kingdom, Alba, was Gaelic-speaking and centered east of the Highlands. Through war and marriage it absorbed the British kingdom of Strathclyde and, after the battle of Carham (1018), English-speaking Lothian, reaching roughly its modern borders. Under Malcolm III and his English queen Margaret, an Anglo-Saxon princess later canonized, and their sons, especially David I (1124-1153), the kingdom was transformed along Norman lines: feudal lordships and castles, royal burghs, reformed coinage and new monasteries such as Melrose and Holyrood.
para2: Relations with England defined the kingdom's history. Scottish kings held lands in England and paid homage for them, but fiercely guarded their independence. When the direct line failed in 1290, Edward I of England arbitrated the succession, chose John Balliol, and then treated Scotland as a vassal. Resistance erupted under William Wallace, victor at Stirling Bridge (1297), defeated at Falkirk (1298) and executed in 1305. Robert the Bruce, after killing his rival John Comyn, seized the throne in 1306 and won independence the hard way, destroying Edward II's army at Bannockburn in 1314. The Declaration of Arbroath (1320) declared to the pope that Scots fought 'not for glory, riches or honours, but for freedom alone', and England recognized the kingdom in 1328.
para3: Under the Stewart dynasty, from Robert II in 1371, Scotland remained a small, poor but stubborn kingdom. Its 'Auld Alliance' with France, from 1295, countered English pressure, and border warfare was endemic; the death of James IV at Flodden (1513) was the worst disaster of the age. Scottish kings struggled to master their own magnates, and several died violently. The 16th century brought the Reformation: in 1560 the Scottish Parliament, led by John Knox and the Lords of the Congregation, established a Protestant kirk, and the Catholic Mary Queen of Scots, driven from her throne, was eventually executed by Elizabeth I of England in 1587.
para4: In 1603 James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne as James I, uniting the crowns while the kingdoms remained legally separate. The century that followed brought civil wars, Covenanter resistance to royal religious policy, and the ruinous Darien colonial scheme (1698-1700). Pressured by economic need and English politics, the Scottish Parliament voted the Acts of Union of 1707, merging Scotland with England into Great Britain and dissolving the old kingdom. Scotland kept its own church, law and education, foundations of a distinct national life that survived the loss of statehood.

title: The Kingdom of Leon
titleline: The Kingdom of Leon - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Leon (910-1230) was the leading Christian kingdom of early medieval Iberia, heir of the Visigothic refugees who had held out in the northern mountains as the Kingdom of Asturias after the Muslim conquest of 711. In 910 Garcia I moved the capital south from Oviedo to the old Roman city of Leon, closer to the frontier, and the kingdom took the city's name. Leonese kings claimed to continue the Visigothic monarchy and pushed the frontier south into the Duero valley, settling it with colonists and building the castle lines, the origin of the name Castile, that guarded it.
para2: The kingdom's fortunes rose and fell with the struggle against Muslim al-Andalus. Almanzor, the all-powerful minister of Cordoba, sacked Leon itself in 988 and devastated the Christian states, but after the caliphate collapsed into taifa kingdoms in 1031, the balance reversed. Ferdinand I (1037-1065) united Leon with Castile, defeated and killed his brother the king of Navarre, and made the taifas of Toledo, Seville and Badajoz pay tribute. His son Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085, the first great Muslim capital to fall, and ruled an empire of 'the two religions'. The Almoravid and then Almohad counterattacks from North Africa, victors at Zallaqa (1086), Ucles (1108) and Alarcos (1195), kept the frontier in blood for another century.
para3: Leon was also a kingdom of pilgrims and laws. The road to Santiago de Compostela ran through its lands, bringing French monks, merchants and settlers and tying the kingdom to European currents of reform and Romanesque art. In 1188 Alfonso IX summoned the Cortes of Leon, which included town representatives alongside nobles and clergy, among the earliest parliaments in Europe to admit the third estate. Its decrees protected property and limited royal power, and Leon developed its own legal tradition, later codified in Castilian law.
para4: The kingdom's unity with Castile repeatedly broke on inheritance: Alfonso VII's empire split between his sons in 1157, and Leon went its own way under Ferdinand II and Alfonso IX. The final reunion came through the remarkable Ferdinand III, who inherited Castile in 1217 and Leon from his father in 1230, this time permanently. Warrior and later saint, Ferdinand conquered Cordoba (1236) and Seville (1248), reducing Muslim power in Iberia to Granada. Thereafter Leon's identity was absorbed into the Crown of Castile, but its laws, its parliament and its old capital remained monuments of the kingdom that carried the Reconquista from the mountains to the Guadalquivir.

title: Al-Andalus under the Caliphate of Cordoba
titleline: Al-Andalus under the Caliphate of Cordoba - The History Web
para1: The Caliphate of Cordoba (929-1031) was the zenith of Muslim al-Andalus, the Iberian lands ruled from 711 by conquerors from North Africa. After the Umayyad caliphate fell in the east, the refugee prince Abd al-Rahman I crossed to Spain in 750, overthrew its governors and founded the Emirate of Cordoba (756). For two centuries his descendants gradually subdued the fractious Arab and Berber elites, defended the frontier against the Christian north and the Fatimids in Africa, and built a centralized administration on Islamic and Persianate lines.
para2: In 929 Abd al-Rahman III took the title of caliph, commander of the faithful, directly challenging the Fatimids in Ifriqiya and the Abbasids in Baghdad. His reign, and that of his son al-Hakam II, marked the caliphate's golden age. Cordoba became the largest and most splendid city in western Europe, with paved streets, markets, hospitals and a famous library of hundreds of thousands of volumes. A school of translators and scholars, physicians, astronomers and poets made it a meeting point of Arabic, Latin, Greek, Jewish and Berber learning. Royal workshops produced ivories and silks prized from France to Egypt, and the caliphs began the palace-city of Madinat al-Zahra outside the capital, a monument of Islamic art and power.
para3: The caliphate's strength rested on a professional army increasingly built on Berber recruits and on purchased slave-soldiers, the saqaliba, whose commanders grew into kingmakers. Al-Hakam II's death in 976 left a child caliph, Hisham II, and real power passed to the brilliant and ruthless chamberlain al-Mansur (Almanzor), who won more than fifty campaigns, sacked Barcelona (985), Leon (988) and even Santiago de Compostela (997). But Almanzor and his sons ruled through the army, and after their deaths (1002, 1008) the system tore itself apart: Berber and saqaliba factions, rival Umayyad claimants and the great cities plunged al-Andalus into the civil war known as the Fitna.
para4: In 1031 the leading families of Cordoba abolished the caliphate altogether, and al-Andalus shattered into the taifa kingdoms. Politically fragmented, Muslim Spain lost Toledo to Alfonso VI of Castile in 1085 and survived only through North African intervention, first by the Almoravids, then the Almohads. Yet the caliphate's cultural legacy outlasted its politics: through Cordoba's scholars, Arabic science, philosophy, medicine and poetry passed into Latin Europe, and the Great Mosque the caliphs enlarged, with its forest of columns and horseshoe arches, still stands as the emblem of al-Andalus.

title: The Taifa Kingdoms
titleline: The Taifa Kingdoms - The History Web
para1: The Taifa kingdoms (1031-1212) were the small Muslim states into which al-Andalus broke after the abolition of the Caliphate of Cordoba. 'Taifa' comes from the Arabic for 'faction' or 'party', and the era saw some three dozen local dynasties, Arab, Berber and saqaliba (slave-soldier) in origin, ruling from the great cities: Seville, Granada, Toledo, Badajoz, Valencia, Zaragoza and others. The breakup followed the Fitna, the civil war unleashed after the death of Almanzor's house, and it left Muslim Spain divided just as the Christian kingdoms of the north were pressing south.
para2: Politically weak, the taifas were culturally brilliant. Courts competed for poets, scholars, scientists and artists, and the eleventh century became a golden age of Andalusi letters: the poet-king al-Mutamid ruled a Seville famous for its salons, Ibn Hazm of Cordoba wrote his treatise on love and his studies of religions, and astronomy, agronomy, philosophy and medicine flourished. The taifa rulers built and beautified palaces such as the Aljaferia of Zaragoza and the Alcazabas of Malaga and Almeria, whose fleets briefly made it the richest port of the western Mediterranean.
para3: The taifas bought security with parias, heavy tribute paid to the Christian kings, a flow of gold that financed the Reconquista and Romanesque building in Leon and Castile. When Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085, al-Mutamid of Seville decided that he would rather 'herd camels for the Almoravids than pigs for Castile', and called in the Almoravids, the austere Berber reform movement ruling Morocco. The Almoravid emir Yusuf ibn Tashfin crushed Alfonso at Zallaqa (1086), then returned, and by 1094 he had annexed the taifas themselves, resentful of their luxury and religious laxity, reuniting al-Andalus under Marrakesh.
para4: Almoravid rule decayed in the next generation, and a second, shorter taifa period followed before the Almohads, a new Berber movement preaching strict monotheism, crossed from Africa after 1147 and subdued Muslim Spain. Almohad power broke on the plain of Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), where the combined armies of Castile, Aragon and Navarre destroyed Caliph al-Nasir's army. Al-Andalus then collapsed into a third round of taifas, which the Christian kingdoms swallowed one by one, Cordoba (1236), Valencia (1238), Seville (1248), until only Granada remained. The taifa age thus frames both the cultural peak of al-Andalus and the turning of the Iberian balance permanently toward the Christian north.

title: The Emirate of Granada
titleline: The Emirate of Granada - The History Web
para1: The Emirate of Granada (1232-1492) was the last Muslim state of the Iberian Peninsula, founded by Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Nasr, called Ibn al-Ahmar, who seized Granada in 1232 and built the Nasrid dynasty that ruled for two and a half centuries. Wedged between the Castilian conquests and the sea, the emirate survived by agility: Ibn al-Ahmar did homage to Ferdinand III of Castile and even helped him take Seville in 1248, in exchange for recognition. Granada became a tribute-paying vassal of Castile, its kings balancing Castile, the Marinids of Morocco, Aragon and their own ambitious frontier clans.
para2: Protected by the Sierra Nevada and a chain of hilltop fortresses, the emirate prospered. It drew wealth from silk, sugar and dried fruit, from the ports of Malaga and Almeria, and from its position on trade routes to Africa and Italy. Refugees from the conquered north doubled its population and enriched its culture. The Nasrids lavished their resources on Granada's palaces, above all the Alhambra, the red-walled palace city begun under Ibn al-Ahmar and completed under Yusuf I and Muhammad V in the 14th century, whose courtyards of the Myrtles and the Lions, with their carved stucco, tile and muqarnas vaults, remain the supreme monument of Islamic art in western Europe. Scholars, poets and Sufis, among them the vizier and historian Ibn al-Khatib, made Granada a final brilliant chapter of Andalusi civilization.
para3: The 15th century brought decline. Succession disputes, the feuds of the powerful Abencerraje clan, and Castile's growing strength after its own civil wars weakened the emirate. Muhammad XI 'the Little' and his successors paid ever heavier tribute, and frontier war, raids, sieges and the loss of strongholds such as Antequera (1410), became routine. The marriage of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile in 1469 united the two great Christian kingdoms, and when the rebel Boabdil (Muhammad XII) fought his father and then his uncle for Granada's throne, the Catholic Monarchs seized their chance.
para4: From 1482 Ferdinand and Isabella ground the emirate down in a ten-year war, taking Ronda, Malaga and Baza piecemeal with superior artillery and resources. Boabdil surrendered Granada on 2 January 1492 and received a small lordship in the Alpujarras before leaving for Morocco. The capitulations promised Muslims their property, law and worship, but these protections were revoked within a decade, and forced conversions, revolts and eventual expulsion of the Moriscos followed. The fall of Granada ended nearly eight centuries of Muslim rule in Iberia, completed the Reconquista, and freed the Catholic Monarchs' resources for the year that also saw Columbus sail and the expulsion of Spain's Jews.

title: The Kingdom of Croatia
titleline: The Kingdom of Croatia - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Croatia (925-1102) emerged from the duchies formed by Croats, a Slavic people who settled the eastern Adriatic in the 7th century, partly under Avar rule. Christianized in the 9th century under Frankish and Byzantine influence, the Croats built an independent duchy under the Trpimirovic dynasty. Duke Branimir won papal recognition in 879, and his successor Tomislav, having defeated the Hungarians on the Drava and the Bulgarians on his southern frontier, was crowned, by tradition with a papal crown, as the first king of Croatia about 925. His realm stretched from the Adriatic islands and coastal cities of Dalmatia to the Pannonian plain.
para2: The kingdom's position between powers shaped its history. Venice, Byzantium, Hungary and the Norman rulers of southern Italy all competed for the Dalmatian cities, which shifted allegiance as the balance moved. Under Peter Kresimir IV (1058-1074) the kingdom reached its greatest extent, holding the coastal towns with Byzantine consent and styling itself the kingdom of the Croats and Dalmatians. The church council of 1060 and 1075 aligned the Croatian church more closely with Rome, insisting on Latin liturgy over the old Slavonic rite, while the Glagolitic script survived in local use.
para3: After the death of Dmitar Zvonimir in 1089 without a clear heir, succession disputes opened the door to outside intervention. The widow Helen, sister of the Hungarian king Ladislaus I, called in her brother, who occupied northern Croatia. The last native king, Peter Svacic, resisted in the mountains until he was defeated and killed, traditionally at Mount Gvozd in 1097. Croatian nobles then negotiated with Ladislaus' successor Coloman, and in 1102, in the settlement known as the Pacta Conventa, they recognized him as king.
para4: The agreement of 1102 created a personal union: Croatia kept its own nobility, laws, diet (the Sabor) and administration under a ban, while sharing a king with Hungary, a link that endured, with interruptions, until 1918. Croatian history was thereafter shaped by Venice, which took most of the Dalmatian cities by 1420, by Hungary's weakness after the Mongol invasion, and from the 15th century by the Ottoman advance, which after Mohacs (1526) brought the Croatian crown to the Habsburgs. The medieval kingdom's memory, Tomislav's crown, the Trpimirovic state, and the Sabor, later anchored Croatian claims to statehood.

title: Wallachia and Moldavia
titleline: Wallachia and Moldavia - The History Web
para1: Wallachia and Moldavia, the two medieval Romanian principalities, formed in the 14th century between the Carpathian Mountains, the Danube and the Black Sea, where Romance-speaking communities, descendants of Romanized provincials, Vlachs, lived under loose Hungarian, Bulgarian and Tatar dominance. Wallachia ('land of the Vlachs') was founded about 1310 by Basarab I, who defied Hungary and routed King Charles Robert at Posada (1330); Moldavia followed in 1359, when Bogdan I threw off Hungarian suzerainty. Ruled by voivodes from the Basarab and Musat dynasties, the principalities held rich salt mines, cattle-raising plains and the Danube trade routes toward the Black Sea ports.
para2: From the later 14th century the Ottoman advance overshadowed both states. Mircea the Elder of Wallachia (1386-1418) fought beside the Crusaders at Nicopolis (1396), survived, and paid tribute to keep his throne while building a strong administration. In Moldavia, Alexander the Good (1400-1432) balanced Poland and the Ottomans, founded churches and monasteries, and gave the principality a stable order. Both rulers used diplomacy, tribute and war in turns, a pattern that preserved autonomy even as Ottoman power surrounded them.
para3: The 15th century produced the principalities' most famous rulers. Vlad III Dracula of Wallachia (1448, 1456-1462, 1476), whose father belonged to the crusading Order of the Dragon, ruled by terror, impaling thousands of enemies and criminals, and struck the Ottomans by night attack at Targoviste (1462) before Mehmed II drove him out; German and Russian pamphlets made his cruelty a legend that later fed the Dracula myth. His contemporary Stephen the Great of Moldavia (1457-1504) fought forty-six battles, defeating the Ottomans at Vaslui (1475), where Pope Sixtus IV named him 'Athlete of Christ', and holding his own against Hungary and Poland; he endowed dozens of the painted monasteries of Bucovina that survive as masterpieces of Byzantine-inherited art.
para4: After Stephen's death both principalities slid into vassalage: they paid tribute, supplied troops, and suffered Ottoman interference in their succession, while keeping their own rulers, laws and armies, a status that preserved Romanian statehood when direct provinces had none. Greek merchants and Phanariot princes later dominated their courts, and Russian and Habsburg pressure grew from the 18th century. The two principalities finally united in 1859 under Alexandru Ioan Cuza, the act that created modern Romania. Their medieval heritage, Orthodox faith with Latin language, boyar landholding, and the monasteries and chronicles of Stephen's and Mircea's age, remains the foundation of Romanian national identity.

title: The Holy Roman Empire after the Interregnum
titleline: The Holy Roman Empire after the Interregnum - The History Web
para1: The death of Emperor Frederick II in 1250 broke imperial power in Germany. The papacy had fought his dynasty to destruction, and after his son Conradin's execution in 1268 no king was recognized for years: foreign princes sold their support for bribes, and the nobility, towns and church states governed themselves. This 'Great Interregnum' (1250-1273) showed that the Holy Roman Empire, the loose federation of hundreds of territories claiming continuity with Rome and Charlemagne, would never again be a centralized monarchy. In 1273 the electors, the great princes who chose the king, picked a minor count, Rudolf of Habsburg, expecting a weak ruler; instead Rudolf defeated Ottokar of Bohemia at Marchfeld (1278) and won Austria, the foundation of his dynasty's power.
para2: A century of experimentation followed. The Swiss cantons broke free of Habsburg lordship at Morgarten (1315); rival kings fought at Muhldorf (1322); and the Wittelsbach emperor Louis IV clashed with the papacy over his very title, defended in writing by Marsilius of Padua's argument that political authority comes from the community, not the pope. What the monarchy lost in power it gained in definition: the imperial crown became effectively elective, and the question was who chose.
para3: The answer came with Charles IV of Luxembourg (1346-1378), king of Bohemia and the empire's greatest late-medieval ruler. In 1356 he issued the Golden Bull, a constitutional charter that fixed the election of the 'King of the Romans' in the hands of seven prince-electors: the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier, and the secular rulers of Bohemia, the Palatinate, Saxony and Brandenburg. The Bull made the electors nearly sovereign in their own lands, gave them regalian rights over mines, tolls and justice, and codified the empire as a federation led by its greatest princes rather than a state ruled from the top.
para4: Under the Golden Bull's framework the empire remained Europe's central political fact for 450 years. Charles IV made Prague an imperial capital, founded its university (1348), the first in central Europe, and built the Charles Bridge; yet after his death his son Wenceslaus was deposed (1400), and the empire faced the Hussite Wars in Bohemia and conciliar crisis in the church. In 1438 the crown passed to Albert II of Habsburg, beginning a Habsburg monopoly that lasted, with one break, until the empire's end in 1806. The late-medieval empire, weak at the center but resilient as a framework, would outlast stronger kingdoms and shape German political life into the modern age.

title: The Crusades
titleline: The Crusades - The History Web
para1: The Crusades (1095-1291) were a series of armed pilgrimages summoned by the Latin Church to recover the Holy Land and defend Christians in the East. In 1095, at the Council of Clermont, Pope Urban II answered the Byzantine emperor Alexios I's appeal for help against the Seljuk Turks with a call for an expedition to free Jerusalem, promising participants remission of penance for their sins. The response astonished Europe: tens of thousands, nobles, knights, clergy and poor pilgrims, 'took the cross'. The First Crusade (1096-1099), led by Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond of Taranto and others, crossed Anatolia, took Antioch after a terrible siege, and stormed Jerusalem in July 1099, massacring much of its population, a brutal beginning that Muslims and Eastern Christians never forgot.
para2: The crusaders established four states in the Levant: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Tripoli, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Edessa, known collectively as Outremer. Thinly ruled by a Frankish warrior elite, they depended on reinforcements from Europe and on the new military orders, the Templars and Hospitallers. Muslim recovery began under Zengi, who took Edessa in 1144, prompting the failed Second Crusade (1147-1149), and climaxed under Saladin, who destroyed the crusader army at Hattin in 1187 and took Jerusalem. That loss launched the Third Crusade (1189-1192): Frederick Barbarossa drowned on the way, Philip II of France went home early, and Richard the Lionheart of England won at Arsuf and Jaffa but could not retake Jerusalem, settling for pilgrim access by treaty.
para3: Later crusades showed the movement's widening and corrupting reach. The Fourth Crusade (1202-1204) was diverted by Venice to sack Christian Constantinople. Innocent III called the Albigensian Crusade (1209-1229) against heretics in southern France, and popes preached crusades in the Baltic, Spain and even against political enemies in Italy. The Fifth Crusade (1217-1221) attacked Egypt and failed; the excommunicated Emperor Frederick II recovered Jerusalem by negotiation in 1229, only to lose it again in 1244; and Louis IX of France led two crusades (1248-1254, 1270), dying on the second outside Tunis. After the fall of Acre in 1291, the mainland crusader states were gone.
para4: The Crusades failed in their central aim, the lasting recovery of the Holy Land, but their effects were enormous. They deepened the split between Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, sharpened Muslim hostility and solidarity, and left a bitter inheritance of holy war. They also accelerated change in Europe: Venetian and Genoese fleets grew rich on crusader shipping, kings taxed and centralized in the crusading cause, the papal monarchy reached its height, and contact with the Islamic world and Byzantium transmitted goods, tastes and learning, sugar, citrus, Arabic science and Greek texts, westward. The memory of the crusades, heroic in Europe, traumatic in the Middle East, still shapes how both remember the age.

title: The Fourth Crusade and the Latin Empire
titleline: The Fourth Crusade and the Latin Empire - The History Web
para1: The Fourth Crusade (1202-1204) was called by Pope Innocent III to strike at Muslim power through Egypt, but it never reached its goal. The crusade's leaders contracted with Venice for transport, promising a payment they could not raise. To work off the debt, the Doge Enrico Dandolo persuaded them to help Venice recover the rebellious city of Zara, a Christian city, in 1202. Then a new temptation appeared: Alexios Angelos, a Byzantine prince, promised the crusaders money, men and the submission of the Greek church to Rome if they would restore his deposed father, Isaac II. Despite the pope's prohibition, the host sailed on Constantinople.
para2: In July 1203 the crusaders stormed Constantinople's sea walls and restored Isaac and Alexios IV, but the promised payments never came, and relations with the Greeks collapsed into street war. When Alexios IV was overthrown and strangled in January 1204, the crusaders, unpaid and now facing a hostile city, decided to take the empire itself. On 13 April 1204 they breached the walls and sacked Constantinople for three days: churches, palaces and libraries were looted, the great bronze horses were carried to St Mark's in Venice, and ancient works of art were melted for coin. The atrocity horrified even Innocent III and poisoned Catholic-Orthodox relations for centuries.
para3: The victors divided the Byzantine world by the Partitio Romaniae: Count Baldwin of Flanders was elected Latin Emperor, ruling a quarter of the old empire from Constantinople, while Venice took the best ports and islands, and crusader lords carved out the Kingdom of Thessalonica, the Principality of Achaea, the Duchy of Athens and other Frankish states. A Latin patriarch replaced the Orthodox hierarchy. But the 'Latin Empire of Constantinople' was poor, undermanned and beset: the Bulgarians crushed Baldwin at Adrianople in 1205, and Greek successor states at Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond claimed the imperial inheritance.
para4: The Latin Empire dwindled to Constantinople and its hinterland, begging in vain for help from the West, pawning even the Crown of Thorns to Venice. In July 1261 the Nicaean general Alexios Strategopoulos retook the city almost without a fight, restoring the Byzantine Empire under Michael VIII Palaiologos. The Frankish states of Greece lasted longer, Achaea and Athens into the 15th century, but the crusade's real legacy was ruinous: Byzantium, still the chief bulwark between Europe and the East, never recovered its old strength, and the path toward 1453 and Ottoman rule in the Balkans was opened.

title: The Mongol Invasions of Europe
titleline: The Mongol Invasions of Europe - The History Web
para1: The Mongol invasions of Europe (1236-1242) were part of the great western campaign ordered by the Great Khan Ogodei and commanded by Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, with the veteran general Subedei as his strategist. After securing the steppe, the Mongols fell on the Volga Bulgars and then on the Rus' principalities: Riazan, Vladimir and Suzdal were stormed and burned in the winter of 1237-1238, and Kiev, the mother city of Rus', fell in December 1240 after a siege. The Russian lands, except Novgorod, became tributaries of the Golden Horde for two centuries, paying tribute and supplying troops to the khans of the Volga.
para2: In the spring of 1241 Batu's army split into columns and struck Poland and Hungary simultaneously. In Silesia, a Polish-German army under Duke Henry II the Pious was annihilated at Legnica (Liegnitz) on 9 April, the duke killed, the Mongols reportedly filling nine sacks with the right ears of the dead. Three days later the main army destroyed King Bela IV of Hungary at Mohi on the Sajo River, using feigned retreat, encirclement and catapults to break the Hungarian host. Hungary lay open: Pest was burned, the plain was ravaged, and perhaps a quarter of its population perished, while Bela fled to the Adriatic and Mongol detachments chased him into Croatia and reached the walls of Vienna's neighborhood.
para3: Latin Europe panicked but did not unite. The emperor Frederick II and the pope were at war, and no crusade materialized; the Mongols faced no coherent western army. Then, in the spring of 1242, Batu unexpectedly withdrew his whole host eastward. The death of Ogodei in December 1241 required the princes to attend the election of a new khan, though scholars also point to Hungary's spring floods, dwindling pasture and the limits of steppe logistics. The Mongols raided the Balkans again, Bulgaria, Serbia and Thrace, and later invaded Poland (1259, 1287) and Hungary (1285) with diminishing success against rebuilt stone castles and prepared armies.
para4: The invasions transformed eastern Europe. Hungary repopulated its plains, walled its towns and welcomed settlers, including Cumans; Poland and the Rus' lands rebuilt under the shadow of the Horde; and the 'Tatar yoke' shaped Russian political development for generations. The terror also opened a door: Europe sent envoys like John of Plano Carpini and William of Rubruck to the khans, merchants like the Polos followed the Mongol peace across Asia, and for a century East and West were in closer contact than ever before. The Golden Horde itself survived on the lower Volga until the 16th century, Islamized, Turkicized, and finally broken among successor khanates.

title: The Black Death
titleline: The Black Death - The History Web
para1: The Black Death (1347-1353) was the deadliest pandemic in recorded history, killing perhaps a third to a half of Europe's people in five years. The disease was plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, carried by fleas living on rodents and spread along trade routes from Central Asia. It reached the Black Sea port of Caffa in 1346-1347, during its siege by the Mongols, and Genoese ships carried it to Sicily in October 1347. Within months it was in Italy, France and Spain; by 1348 in England and the Balkans; by 1350 in Germany, Scandinavia and Russia. It returned in repeated waves for four centuries.
para2: Contemporaries described buboes, swollen lymph nodes in groin and armpit, black blotches, spitting blood and death within days; the pneumonic form killed even faster. No remedy worked. Cities lost half their populations; some villages were emptied entirely. Chroniclers like Boccaccio, who watched Florence die and framed the Decameron around it, wrote of parents abandoning children and bodies buried in trenches. Medicine of the day blamed corrupted air, and authorities responded with flight, prayer, quarantines, Ragusa (Dubrovnik) enforced isolation in 1377, and, in some regions, violence: Jewish communities were accused of poisoning wells and massacred in cities from the Rhineland to Spain despite papal condemnation.
para3: The economic consequences reshaped Europe. With a third of the workforce gone, survivors' labor became valuable: wages rose, rents and grain prices fell, and serfs bargained for freedom or fled to towns, accelerating the end of serfdom in western Europe. Landlords answered with repression, England's Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to freeze wages, and the tension exploded in the English Peasants' Revolt (1381), the French Jacquerie (1358) and urban risings in Flanders and Italy. Whole villages were abandoned to pasture, marginal lands reverted to forest, and sheep farming expanded where fields no longer paid.
para4: The cultural and religious effects were as deep. The flagellant movement marched from town to town seeking to avert God's wrath; the church, whose clergy died at high rates tending the sick, lost moral authority; art turned morbid, the danse macabre and memento mori became common motifs. Scholars have long debated links between the plague and the loosening of medieval certainties that fed the Renaissance and, later, calls for church reform. The Black Death did not create the late medieval world, but by thinning population, raising the value of labor and shaking institutions, it hastened the end of the medieval order and the birth of the early modern one.

title: The Hussite Wars
titleline: The Hussite Wars - The History Web
para1: The Hussite Wars (1419-1434) were a series of conflicts in Bohemia sparked by the execution of the reformer Jan Hus. Hus, a Prague preacher and university master inspired by John Wyclif, attacked indulgences, clerical wealth and the worldly power of the church, and demanded that laypeople receive communion in both kinds, bread and wine, symbolized by the chalice that became the Hussite emblem. Summoned to the Council of Constance under a safe conduct from King Sigismund, he was imprisoned, condemned for heresy and burned on 6 July 1415. Bohemia erupted: nobles formed a league to defend free preaching, and in July 1419 Prague radicals threw the Catholic town councillors from the New Town Hall windows, the first Defenestration of Prague.
para2: The Hussites were never one party. The moderate Utraquists of Prague wanted chiefly the chalice for the laity and church reform within the old framework; the radical Taborites, gathered at their new fortress-town of Tabor, rejected most of the inherited church order and awaited God's kingdom; smaller groups went further. All united against King Sigismund, heir of the hated council and brother of the dead King Wenceslaus IV, whose claim to the Bohemian crown they refused. Under the one-eyed Jan Zizka, the Hussites developed a revolutionary way of war: laagered wagon forts chained together, manned by peasant infantry with flails, pikes and handguns, supported by field artillery, tactics that defeated mounted knights again and again.
para3: Five crusades were preached against Bohemia (1420, 1421, 1422, 1427, 1431), and all failed. Zizka, though fully blind from 1421, crushed the first two, winning at Vitkov Hill, Kutna Hora and Nemecky Brod; after his death in 1424 the Taborite general Prokop the Great carried the war into Germany, Austria and Silesia in 'beautiful rides' that terrified central Europe. The fifth crusade broke at Domazlice (Taus) in 1431 at the mere rumor of the Hussite wagons, and the church changed course: at the Council of Basel it negotiated the Compactata (1436), granting the Utraquists communion in both kinds, the first time the medieval church made doctrinal concessions to a reform movement under pressure.
para4: The radicals would not compromise. In 1434 the Utraquist nobles and Prague, allied with Catholics, destroyed the Taborite and Orphan armies at Lipany, where Prokop fell. Bohemia kept its Hussite character under King George of Podebrady (1458-1471), a Utraquist 'king of two peoples', and the Compactata remained Bohemia's religious settlement for two centuries. The Hussites left a lasting mark: they anticipated themes of the Reformation, gave Bohemia a distinct national and religious identity, revolutionized infantry warfare with wagons and gunpowder, and inspired later movements, the Moravian Brethren among them, that carried Hus's memory into the modern world.

title: The Fall of Constantinople
titleline: The Fall of Constantinople - The History Web
para1: The Fall of Constantinople on 29 May 1453 ended the Byzantine Empire after more than eleven centuries. By then the empire had shrunk to the capital, a few Aegean outposts and the Morea, its population a fraction of its former size. The young Ottoman sultan Mehmed II, determined to take the city that guarded the junction of Europe and Asia, prepared methodically: he built the fortress of Rumeli Hisari on the Bosporus to cut the city from the Black Sea, gathered an army of perhaps 80,000, and commissioned from the engineer Orban bronze cannon of unprecedented size, bombards that could batter the ancient Theodosian Walls, which had stood unconquered for a thousand years.
para2: Against this, Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos could field only about 7,000 defenders, including 700 Genoese under Giovanni Giustiniani, a few Venetians, Catalans and Cretans, and the crews of the ships sheltering behind the great chain that closed the Golden Horn. The siege began on 6 April 1453. Ottoman guns pounded the walls near the Gate of St Romanus; a daring night attack on the boom failed; four Genoese supply ships beat the entire Ottoman fleet in a famous action; but the defenders' numbers told. Mehmed had ships dragged overland into the Golden Horn, bypassing the chain, forcing the city to stretch its thin line even thinner.
para3: After seven weeks of bombardment, and rejected terms that would have spared the city, Mehmed launched the general assault before dawn on 29 May. Wave after wave of irregulars, Anatolian troops and finally the elite Janissaries tested the breaches; Giustiniani was wounded and carried off, the defense wavered, and Ottoman troops found their way in through a small sally port, the Kerkoporta, left unsecured. Constantine XI died in the fighting, last of the Roman emperors. The city was given over to three days of sack, as custom allowed, its people killed or enslaved, its churches and palaces stripped, though Mehmed soon called a halt and began restoring his prize.
para4: Constantinople became the Ottoman capital, Istanbul, and Hagia Sophia its chief mosque. The fall resonated far beyond the city: Greek scholars had already carried manuscripts and learning westward, feeding the Renaissance; Orthodox Moscow later styled itself the 'Third Rome'; popes preached crusades that never came; and Europe understood that Ottoman power was now planted permanently in the Balkans. The date 1453 is conventionally taken to close the Middle Ages, not because the world changed in a day, but because the last direct link to ancient Rome, the empire Augustus founded, had finally disappeared.

title: The Kingdom of Denmark-Norway
titleline: The Kingdom of Denmark-Norway - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Denmark-Norway (1523-1814) was the dual monarchy formed when Gustav Vasa's rebellion dissolved the Kalmar Union in 1523, leaving Denmark and Norway, with Iceland, Greenland and the Faroe Islands, under the Oldenburg kings of Denmark. Norway was by far the weaker partner: its council faded, its administration filled with Danish officials, and in 1537 it was formally declared a dependency of the Danish crown. From Copenhagen, the kings ruled a composite state that also included the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein, and which competed with Sweden for control of the Baltic, the Sound tolls on passing shipping being the monarchy's richest revenue.
para2: The 16th century was the monarchy's golden age. Frederick I and Christian III accepted the Lutheran Reformation in 1536, confiscating the wealthy church lands into the crown; Christian III rebuilt the navy and fortified the Sound. Frederick II and Christian IV, builder of Rosenborg Castle and the Bourse, presided over a flourishing trade and a court famous for music, science, Tycho Brahe observed the heavens from his island of Hven, and culture. But Christian IV's ambition overreached: the Kalmar War (1611-1613) with Sweden ended indecisively, and his intervention in the Thirty Years' War (1625-1629) was crushed by Wallenstein's armies.
para3: The 17th century turned catastrophic. In the Torstenson War (1643-1645) Denmark lost Jemtland, Herjedalen and Gotland; worse came in 1658, when Charles X Gustav of Sweden marched his army across the frozen Belts in one of history's boldest maneuvers, forcing the Peace of Roskilde, which ceded Scania, Halland, Blekinge and Bornholm's neighbors, Denmark's richest provinces east of the Sound. The shock produced a domestic revolution: in 1660 the estates gave Frederick III absolute and hereditary power, making Denmark-Norway Europe's most formally absolute monarchy, governed by the Lex Regia of 1665. The crown then rebuilt: a new navy, mercantile colonies in Africa, India and the Caribbean, and an efficient centralized bureaucracy.
para4: Denmark-Norway regained nothing from Sweden despite fighting in the Scanian War (1675-1679) and the Great Northern War (1700-1721), and the 18th century brought prosperity through neutral trade, Enlightenment reform under ministers such as the Struensee episode and then Crown Prince Frederick's regency, and the abolition of serfdom in 1788. The Napoleonic Wars destroyed the state: Britain attacked neutral Copenhagen twice (1801, 1807) and seized the fleet, and in 1814 Denmark ceded Norway to Sweden by the Treaty of Kiel, keeping only the North Atlantic islands. Norway promptly declared independence, wrote Europe's most liberal constitution, and entered a union with Sweden that lasted until 1905.

title: The First Kingdom of Burgundy
titleline: The First Kingdom of Burgundy - The History Web
para1: The First Kingdom of Burgundy (413-534) was founded by the Burgundians, an East Germanic people who had migrated from the Baltic across central Europe and settled on the middle Rhine. In 413 their king Gundahar, the Gunther of later legend, established a kingdom at Worms with Roman agreement, serving as federate allies. The kingdom did not last: in 436 Roman magister Aetius unleashed Hunnic auxiliaries against it, destroyed Gundahar and much of his people in a catastrophe later remembered in the Nibelungenlied, and the survivors were resettled in Sapaudia, the region of Lake Geneva and the upper Rhone, in 443.
para2: From Sapaudia the Burgundians expanded into the vacuum left by collapsing Roman power in Gaul. Under King Gundobad (c. 474-516), who had begun his career as a Roman patrician in Italy, the kingdom reached from Lyon down the Rhone to the Mediterranean. The Burgundians ruled as a small warrior minority over a large Gallo-Roman population, sharing lands with them by the customary hospitalitas system, and the two peoples gradually merged. Burgundian kings patronized the church, though they were long Arian Christians among Catholic subjects, and the monasteries of the Rhone valley flourished.
para3: Gundobad is remembered above all as a lawgiver. His Lex Burgundionum, issued around the turn of the 6th century, codified the customs of both Burgundians and Romans in his realm, and a parallel Roman law book served his Gallo-Roman subjects, making the kingdom a leader among the successor states in written law. His court at Lyon and Geneva also produced the first major historian of the Franks' neighbors, and his letters show a king trying to balance Roman tradition with Germanic kingship.
para4: After Gundobad's death the kingdom weakened under his son Sigismund, who converted to Catholicism and founded the great abbey of Saint-Maurice d'Agaune, and his brother Godomar. The Frankish kings, sons of Clovis, saw their chance: in 523 they invaded, captured and executed Sigismund, and after Godomar's resistance, annexed the whole kingdom in 534. Burgundy survived as a name and an idea, first as a Frankish sub-kingdom, later as the middle kingdom of Lotharingia's partition, then as the Kingdom of Arles and the famous French duchy, but the independent Burgundian people dissolved into the populations of Gaul, leaving their name on the map of France and their law code in its legal tradition.

title: The Duchy of Burgundy
titleline: The Duchy of Burgundy - The History Web
para1: The Duchy of Burgundy (918-1482) began as a Carolingian border province granted in 918 to Richard the Justiciar, and from 1032 it was ruled by a branch of the French royal house. For centuries it was one of several French principalities, its dukes vassals of the king of France, with the Free County of Burgundy (Franche-Comte) across the Saone belonging instead to the Holy Roman Empire. The duchy was transformed when the direct Capetian line of dukes ended in 1361: King John II of France granted it to his youngest son Philip 'the Bold' (1364-1404), founding the Valois-Burgundian dynasty that would nearly create a middle kingdom between France and Germany.
para2: Philip the Bold married the heiress of Flanders, adding the richest trading towns of northern Europe to Burgundian rule, and his successors piled inheritance on inheritance: John the Fearless (1404-1419), whose murder of the Duke of Orleans plunged France into civil war and who was himself assassinated on the bridge of Montereau; and Philip the Good (1419-1467), who allied with England during the Hundred Years' War, captured Joan of Arc at Compiegne, and added Holland, Zeeland, Hainaut, Brabant, Limburg and Luxembourg. Under Philip the Burgundian court at Dijon, Bruges and Brussels became the most splendid in Europe: painters like Jan van Eyck and Rogier van der Weyden, the musicians of the Burgundian school, the lavish banquets of the Order of the Golden Fleece, founded 1430, and a library of illuminated manuscripts rivaled only by kings.
para3: The dynasty's last and most ambitious duke, Charles the Bold (1467-1477), set out to weld his scattered lands, Burgundy, Franche-Comte and the Low Countries, into a continuous kingdom by conquering Lorraine, the corridor between them. He clashed with Louis XI of France, who coordinated a web of enemies against him, and with the Swiss Confederates, allied to Lorraine and France. Charles took Nancy and Grandson, but in 1476 the Swiss destroyed his army at Grandson, seizing his fabulous artillery and treasure, crushed him again at Morat with enormous slaughter, and in January 1477 killed him before the walls of Nancy, his body found frozen in a ditch.
para4: Charles left only a daughter, Mary of Burgundy. Louis XI seized the duchy and Picardy by force, while Mary saved the Low Countries by marrying Maximilian of Habsburg; she died in 1482, leaving her inheritance to her son Philip the Fair. The settlement split the Burgundian legacy: the French crown kept Burgundy proper, the Habsburgs took Franche-Comte and the Netherlands, and Franco-Habsburg rivalry over that inheritance dominated European wars for two centuries. The Valois dukes had failed to found a kingdom, but their court set the standards of European splendor, and their Low Countries became the heartland of Habsburg power.

title: The Kingdom of Navarre
titleline: The Kingdom of Navarre - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Navarre (824-1512), originally the Kingdom of Pamplona, was the Basque kingdom of the western Pyrenees. Its founder Inigo Arista threw off Frankish overlordship about 824, and under the Jimenez dynasty the kingdom grew into the greatest Christian power in Spain: Sancho III 'the Great' (1004-1035) ruled Navarre, Castile, Aragon and much of Leon, patronized the pilgrimage road to Compostela, and on his death divided his lands among his sons, creating the kingdoms of Castile and Aragon. Thereafter Navarre was the smallest of the Iberian kingdoms, surviving between its larger neighbors through diplomacy and the defense of its Pyrenean passes.
para2: The kingdom was a meeting place: Basques in the western valleys, Romance-speakers in the Ebro plain, plus important Jewish and Muslim communities, all under laws, the fueros, that limited royal power. From 1234 Navarre passed to French dynasties, the counts of Champagne and then the Capetian house, and from 1284 to 1328 its kings were also kings of France. French rule brought administrators, Gothic building and closer ties northward, but also resentment. Under Charles II 'the Bad' (1349-1387), a schemer of genius with a claim to the French throne, Navarre played England against France throughout the Hundred Years' War, holding Normandy as well as the Pyrenean kingdom until his son Charles III 'the Noble' made peace and gave Navarre a final age of prosperity, law-giving and splendid building at Olite.
para3: The 15th century weakened Navarre fatally. The throne passed to the house of Trastamara and then Foix, entangling the kingdom in Aragonese politics, and civil war broke out between two noble factions, the Agramonts and Beaumonts, while the kingdom's French and Iberian neighbors circled. Ferdinand II of Aragon, having married Isabella of Castile, intervened in Navarre's civil strife, and in 1512 his armies conquered the kingdom south of the Pyrenees, invoking a papal bull. The Navarrese Cortes resisted, and King Catherine and John III kept only tiny Lower Navarre north of the mountains.
para4: Spanish Navarre kept its own fueros, Cortes and administration within the Crown of Castile and later Spain, a distinct legal existence that lasted into the 19th century. The remnant north of the Pyrenees eventually passed to Henry of Bourbon, who in 1589 became Henry IV of France, uniting the old kingdom's name to the French crown. Navarre's history, the smallest Iberian kingdom, yet mother of Castile and Aragon, and the crucible where Basque, Spanish and French worlds met, left an outsized mark on both Spain and France.

title: The Serbian Kingdom before the Empire
titleline: The Serbian Kingdom before the Empire - The History Web
para1: The medieval Serbian Kingdom arose from the zupas, small Slavic principalities of the central Balkans, which had passed between Byzantine, Bulgarian and Frankish influence since the 7th century. Its founder was Stefan Nemanja, grand zupan of Raska from 1166, who united the Serbian lands, took advantage of Emperor Manuel I's death to break from Byzantium, and annexed Zeta (Montenegro) and lands toward the Adriatic. Nemanja allied at times with Hungary, Venice and the Normans, fought the Bulgarians and the emperor Isaac II, and in 1196 abdicated in favor of his son Stefan and withdrew to Mount Athos as the monk Simeon, founder with his youngest son Rastko, Saint Sava, of the Serbian monastery of Hilandar.
para2: Sava gave the kingdom its church. After the crusaders' sack of Constantinople in 1204 shattered Byzantine control, he secured in 1219 from the exiled patriarch at Nicaea an autocephalous Serbian archbishopric, and organized its dioceses, wrote its first laws, and anchored national life in the monasteries, Zica, Studenica, Mileseva, whose frescoes are masterpieces of Byzantine-inherited art. His brother Stefan, crowned in 1217 with a crown sent by the pope, became the 'First-Crowned' king; Serbia thereafter balanced between Rome and Constantinople, marrying into both worlds while keeping the Orthodox faith.
para3: The 13th-century kingdom prospered on its silver mines, Novo Brdo and Srebrenica among the richest in Europe, worked by Saxon miners, and on the trade of Ragusa (Dubrovnik). Kings Uros I and Dragutin extended Serbian rule south into Macedonia at Byzantine expense, and King Milutin (1282-1321) pushed deep into Byzantine Macedonia, taking Skopje as his capital and building churches from Gracanica to Studenica that mark the golden age of medieval Serbian art. Milutin married the emperor's daughter and styled himself almost a Byzantine ruler, and his court rivaled Constantinople in ceremony.
para4: The stage was set for Stefan Dusan (1331-1355), Milutin's grandson, who exploited the Byzantine civil wars to conquer most of Albania, Epirus, Macedonia and Thessaly, and in 1346 had himself crowned 'Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks', raising the Serbian church to a patriarchate. His Serbian Empire, the largest state in the Balkans, promulgated Dusan's Code (1349), a major monument of medieval law. It did not outlive him: Dusan died in 1355 marching, some said, on Constantinople, his son Uros 'the Weak' could not hold the magnates, and the empire fragmented into lordships that faced the advancing Ottomans alone, falling one by one after Maritsa (1371) and Kosovo (1389). The Nemanjic kingdom's legacy, its church, monasteries and law, became the core of Serbian national memory.

title: The Florentine Republic
titleline: The Florentine Republic - The History Web
para1: The Florentine Republic (1115-1532) grew from a medieval commune that won effective self-government in the 12th century and dominated Tuscany for four hundred years. Its wealth came from wool and banking: Florentine companies, the Bardi, Peruzzi and later the Medici, financed popes and kings from London to Naples, and the city's gold florin, first minted in 1252, became the standard coin of European trade. Florence was also violently divided: the 13th-century struggle of Guelfs and Ghibellines, and then of Black and White Guelfs, the feud that exiled the poet Dante Alighieri in 1302, gave the commune a politics of faction, exile and confiscation.
para2: The constitution rested on the guilds: the seven 'greater' guilds of bankers, cloth-merchants and lawyers, and the 'lesser' guilds of craftsmen, whose priors formed the Signoria, chosen by lot for two-month terms in the Palazzo Vecchio. Popular risings, the Ciompi revolt of wool-workers in 1378, and the reaction that crushed it, showed how narrow that republic could be, yet the ideal of civic liberty defined Florentine identity. In 1434 Cosimo de' Medici, 'the Elder', returned from exile and mastered the city without any title: through banking wealth, clientage, control of elections and the purse, he and his house guided the republic for sixty years.
para3: Under Cosimo's grandson Lorenzo 'the Magnificent' (1469-1492), Florence was the capital of the Renaissance. Lorenzo held the state through the councils while posing as a private citizen, survived the Pazzi conspiracy of 1478, in which his brother Giuliano was murdered in the cathedral, and the war with Pope Sixtus IV that followed, and balanced the Italian powers through personal diplomacy. His court and commissions gathered Botticelli, the young Michelangelo, Leonardo, Poliziano and Pico della Mirandola; the Platonic Academy, the Laurentian Library and the workshops of the city made Florence the standard of European culture. After Lorenzo's death his son Piero blundered before the invading French in 1494, and the Medici were expelled.
para4: The last phase of the republic was its most turbulent: the Dominican friar Girolamo Savonarola led a puritan popular republic that burned the 'vanities' in 1497 and was himself burned in 1498; the chancellor Niccolo Machiavelli organized a citizen militia and wrote the works that founded modern political thought from the republic's ruins. The Medici returned in 1512 with Spanish arms, were again expelled in 1527, and finally besieged Florence into surrender in 1530. In 1532 the republic was abolished and Alessandro de' Medici made hereditary duke, and in 1569 the Medici became Grand Dukes of Tuscany. The republic fell, but its civic humanism, art and banking techniques had already reshaped Europe.

title: The Duchy of Milan
titleline: The Duchy of Milan - The History Web
para1: The Duchy of Milan (1395-1535) grew from the signoria of the Visconti family, lords of Milan since Archbishop Ottone seized power in 1277. The Visconti built a state in Lombardy through force and marriage, and Giangaleazzo Visconti (1378-1402) carried it furthest: he conquered Verona, Vicenza, Padua, Pisa, Siena and much of Umbria, bought the hereditary title of Duke of Milan from the emperor Wenceslaus in 1395, and was advancing on Florence when he died of plague. His duchy was the most modern government in Italy, with salaried officials, systematic taxation, canals and the beginnings of the Duomo and the Certosa of Pavia.
para2: After Giangaleazzo's death the conquests fell away and had to be retaken by his ruthless son Filippo Maria (1412-1447), the last Visconti duke, who ruled through condottieri, mercenary captains such as Francesco Bussone, called the Carmagnola, and Francesco Sforza. When Filippo Maria died leaving only a daughter, Milan proclaimed the short-lived Ambrosian Republic (1447-1450), which hired Sforza to defend it; Sforza starved the city into surrender instead and entered Milan as duke in 1450. The Sforza dukes, Francesco, Galeazzo Maria, murdered in church in 1476, and the usurper Ludovico 'il Moro', made Milan a center of Renaissance splendor: Ludovico employed Leonardo da Vinci, who painted The Last Supper for the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie, and Bramante rebuilt the city's churches.
para3: It was Ludovico who opened Italy to invasion. Threatened by the Aragonese of Naples, he encouraged Charles VIII of France to claim the Neapolitan throne in 1494, beginning the Italian Wars. The French discovered they liked Milan better than its duke: in 1499 Louis XII, himself a Visconti descendant, took the duchy, and Ludovico died a prisoner in France (1508). For thirty-five years Milan was the chief prize of the wars between Valois France and Habsburg Spain, passing between them at Pavia (1525), where Francis I was captured, and through the Sack of Rome's aftermath.
para4: In 1535 the last Sforza duke died childless, and Emperor Charles V annexed Milan, granting it to his son Philip of Spain in 1540. Spanish Milan, ruled by governors from the Castello Sforzesco, remained the keystone of Habsburg Italy for 170 years, famed for its citadel, its taxes and St Charles Borromeo's reforming archbishopric. The duchy's legacy is the Lombard state it created: canals and rice fields, the great cathedral, and the model of centralized territorial government that other Italian states, and their conquerors, imitated.

title: The Kingdom of Naples
titleline: The Kingdom of Naples - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Naples (1282-1504) was born from the Sicilian Vespers, the revolt that in 1282 expelled the Angevin French from Sicily and broke the kingdom of southern Italy in two: the Aragonese took Sicily, while the Angevins kept the mainland, which came to be called, from its capital, the Kingdom of Naples. Under Robert 'the Wise' (1309-1343), patron of Petrarch and Boccaccio, Naples was a center of early Renaissance culture and Guelf politics, but the dynasty dissolved into murder and succession crisis under his granddaughter Joanna I, who was deposed and killed by her cousin Charles of Durazzo (1382), while the popes, the kingdom's overlords, backed now one claimant, now another.
para2: The Angevin-Durazzo line exhausted itself in these wars, and in 1442 Alfonso V of Aragon, already king of Sicily, took Naples after a long struggle. 'Alfonso the Magnanimous' made the city his capital and one of the great courts of the Renaissance: he rebuilt the Castel Nuovo with its triumphal arch, gathered scholars like Lorenzo Valla and Panormita, and governed Italy through alliances that anticipated the balance of power. At his death in 1458 Sicily and Aragon went to his brother, while Naples passed to his illegitimate son Ferdinand I (Ferrante), whose barons rebelled with Angevin and papal support and were defeated only after years of war; Ferrante's reprisals, including the massacre of barons invited to a wedding feast, made his name a byword for cunning despotism.
para3: The kingdom's weakness invited invasion. The old Angevin claim passed to the French crown, and in 1494 Charles VIII of France marched the length of Italy and took Naples almost unopposed, chased out within a year by the Holy League. Louis XII of France returned in 1501, partitioning the kingdom with Ferdinand the Catholic of Aragon, but the partners fell out, and the Spanish general Gonzalo de Cordoba, 'the Great Captain', destroyed the French armies at Cerignola and on the Garigliano (1503). By 1504 Naples was Spanish.
para4: For two centuries the kingdom was governed by Spanish viceroys, one of the richest and most heavily taxed provinces of the Habsburg monarchy, its barons' estates and grain feeding the empire's wars. The medieval kingdom left a double mark: the south's incorporation into the Spanish imperial system, which shaped its society until 1860, and the brilliant court culture of Angevin and Aragonese Naples, from Boccaccio's decade at Robert's court to the humanist academy of Alfonso, that made the city for a time a capital of European letters.

title: The Burgundian Wars
titleline: The Burgundian Wars - The History Web
para1: The Burgundian Wars (1474-1477) destroyed the Valois Burgundian state of Charles the Bold, the last and most ambitious of the Burgundian dukes. Charles ruled a wealthy chain of territories from Flanders to Franche-Comte and dreamed of welding them into a kingdom between France and Germany. His relentless expansion, the seizure of Alsace, wars on the Rhine, and pressure on Lorraine, alarmed both King Louis XI of France, his feudal overlord and mortal enemy, and the Swiss Confederation, whose trade and security his plans threatened. Louis wove the coalition that would ruin him: the League of Constance (1474) united the Swiss, the Alsatian towns, and Sigismund of Austria against Burgundy.
para2: Charles besieged the small Alsatian town of Neuss (1474-1475), wasting a campaigning season while an imperial army gathered, and had to withdraw. He then conquered Lorraine (1475) and turned on the Swiss, whom his agents and garrisons had provoked beyond endurance. The war that followed was a catastrophe for Burgundy. At Grandson (March 1476) the Swiss infantry routed his magnificent army and captured its artillery and his fabulous camp treasure; at Morat (June 1476), after Charles had rebuilt his forces, the Swiss destroyed his army in an hour and massacred the survivors, leaving thousands dead around the lake.
para3: Charles would not yield. He raised a third army and besieged Nancy, the capital of the revolted Lorraine, in midwinter. On 5 January 1477 the Swiss and Lorrainers attacked in a snowstorm, the Burgundian army collapsed, and Charles's naked body was found two days later in a frozen ditch, the head split by a halberd. He was thirty-three. The death of the last Valois duke of Burgundy ended the Burgundian state as an independent power: Louis XI seized the duchy of Burgundy itself and Picardy, arguing it was a lapsed fief, while Charles's daughter Mary preserved the rest by marrying Maximilian of Habsburg in August 1477.
para4: The settlement took a generation: the Treaty of Arras (1482) and Senlis (1493) divided the inheritance between France and the Habsburgs. France kept the duchy; Maximilian's son Philip the Fair carried the Netherlands and Franche-Comte to the Habsburgs, and through his marriage to Joanna of Castile to the Spanish crown. The Burgundian Wars thus fixed the Franco-Habsburg frontier that would dominate European wars for three centuries, made the reputation of the Swiss pike square, the most feared infantry of the age, and ended the possibility of a middle kingdom between France and Germany.

title: The Wars of the Roses
titleline: The Wars of the Roses - The History Web
para1: The Wars of the Roses (1455-1487) were a series of civil wars between the rival branches of the English royal house, the Lancastrians, symbolized by the red rose, and the Yorkists, by the white. The underlying cause was the weakness of Henry VI of Lancaster, pious, gentle and intermittently insane, whose government lost the Hundred Years' War in France and fell into debt, while rival magnates, over-mighty subjects with private retinues, fought for control of the court. The dynastic question opened in 1460 when Richard, Duke of York, heir presumptive after the birth of Henry's son displaced him, claimed the throne itself as the senior descendant of Edward III.
para2: The first war began at St Albans in 1455. Yorkist and Lancastrian fortunes swung violently: York himself was killed at Wakefield (1460), but his son Edward, Earl of March, crushed the Lancastrians at Towton (1461), the bloodiest battle fought on English soil, and was crowned Edward IV. Margaret of Anjou, Henry VI's formidable queen, kept resistance alive in exile until Edward won twice in 1471, at Barnet, where the turncoat Earl of Warwick, the 'Kingmaker', died, and at Tewkesbury, where the Lancastrian Prince Edward was killed. Henry VI died in the Tower days later, and the Yorkist dynasty seemed secure.
para3: Edward IV ruled capably until his sudden death in 1483, leaving two young sons. His brother Richard, Duke of Gloucester, seized the throne as Richard III, declared the princes illegitimate, and imprisoned them in the Tower of London, where they disappeared, almost certainly murdered. The usurpation split the Yorkist party and opened the way for an improbable claimant: Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, whose claim to the Lancastrian inheritance ran through the legitimized Beaufort line. In August 1485 Henry landed in Wales, gathered support, and killed Richard III at Bosworth Field, where the king, betrayed by the Stanleys, died fighting. Henry was crowned Henry VII on the battlefield.
para4: Henry VII ended the wars by marriage and management. He married Elizabeth of York, uniting the two houses in the Tudor rose, and defeated the last serious Yorkist rising, the pretender Lambert Simnel, at Stoke Field (1487), often counted as the wars' true end. His reign then systematically broke the over-mighty subjects: retainers were restricted by law, royal finance rebuilt, and dynastic rivals executed. The old military aristocracy that had made and unmade kings for thirty years emerged decimated and cowed, and the Wars of the Roses left England a stronger, more centralized monarchy under the Tudors than it had been under the Plantagenets.
