title: The Italian Wars
titleline: The Italian Wars - The History Web
para1: The Italian Wars (1494-1559) were a series of conflicts fought on Italian soil, above all between the French Valois and the Habsburgs, that made Italy the battlefield of Europe for two generations. They began when Charles VIII of France, claiming the Kingdom of Naples through Angevin inheritance, marched down the peninsula in 1494 with modern siege artillery that battered medieval walls into rubble and briefly took Naples. His invasion shattered the Italian balance of power maintained since the Peace of Lodi (1454) among Milan, Venice, Florence, the Papacy and Naples, and it summoned the first of many anti-French coalitions, the League of Venice (1495), which forced Charles home.
para2: The wars widened under Charles's successors. Louis XII seized Milan (1499) and Naples (1501) but lost both after the Holy League of 1511, organized by the combative Pope Julius II, drove France from Milan; the French returned under the young Francis I, whose victory at Marignano (1515) retook Milan and set up the great duel of the age between Francis and the Habsburg Charles V, who from 1519 combined Spain, the Netherlands, Austria and the Empire. After years of campaigning in Lombardy, Francis was captured at Pavia (1525), the decisive battle of the wars, where Spanish shot and pike destroyed the French army and its king.
para3: Pavia opened the war's ugliest phase. Released under the Treaty of Madrid (1526), Francis promptly repudiated it and joined the League of Cognac with the pope; Charles's unpaid imperial army, partly Lutheran landsknechts, mutinied and sacked Rome in May 1527, massacring citizens and holding Pope Clement VII prisoner, an atrocity that shocked Christendom. The French were expelled from Naples after a last failed siege (1528), and the Peace of Cambrai (1529) and, after two more wars, the truce of Nice (1538) settled the peninsula under Spanish control: Milan and Naples were Habsburg, the Medici ruled Florence and Siena, and French attempts under Francis and Henry II to return failed, at Saint-Quentin in 1557 catastrophically.
para4: The Peace of Cateau-Cambresis (1559) ended the wars, confirming Spanish hegemony in Italy that would last a century and a half. Italy's independent political life was strangled: only Venice kept real freedom. Yet the wars spread the Italian Renaissance northward, French, Spanish and imperial soldiers and courts carried home Italian art, architecture, learning and manners, while demonstrating the new age of warfare: artillery fortresses, professional pike-and-shot infantry, and diplomacy as a permanent tool, with resident ambassadors invented in Italy now spreading across Europe. The Franco-Habsburg rivalry the wars fixed would shape European politics until the eighteenth century.

title: The Kingdom of Portugal
titleline: The Kingdom of Portugal - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Portugal emerged in the twelfth century from the County of Portugal, a fief of the kingdom of Leon-Castile granted to Henry of Burgundy in 1096. His son, Afonso Henriques, defeated his own mother's forces at Sao Mamede (1128), won a famous victory over the Almoravids at Ourique (1139), and after it styled himself king. Leon accepted the title by the Treaty of Zamora (1143), and the papacy, won over by his crusading participation in the Reconquista, recognized his kingship in 1179. Afonso's conquest of Lisbon in 1147, with the help of English and Flemish crusaders bound for the Second Crusade, gave the new kingdom its future capital.
para2: Under Afonso's successors the kingdom pushed south at the expense of the Muslim taifas, the frontier fortified by the crusading military orders, the Templars and the Portuguese Order of Avis. The advance was checked by the Almohad caliphs but resumed after their collapse, and in 1249 Afonso III captured Faro, completing the Portuguese Reconquista. Portugal thus fixed its borders, roughly unchanged to the present, earlier than any other European kingdom, which freed it from peninsular entanglements. The reign of Dinis (1279-1325) consolidated the state: he founded the University of Lisbon (1290), made Portuguese the language of administration, built castles and the pine forests of Leiria, and developed agriculture and commerce.
para3: After a dynastic crisis in 1383-1385, when Castile claimed the crown, the master of Avis, Joao I, won the throne with the backing of Lisbon's people, beating Castile at Aljubarrota (1385), and founded the Aviz dynasty. His alliance with England, sealed by the Treaty of Windsor (1386), endures as one of the oldest diplomatic alliances in the world. His sons, including Prince Henry the Navigator, began Portugal's oceanic enterprise: Ceuta was taken in 1415, Madeira and the Azores settled, and Portuguese caravels worked down the African coast. Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, and within decades Portugal commanded a seaborne trading empire from Brazil to the Moluccas.
para4: The empire's wealth funded the golden age of Manuel I, the Manueline style of the Jeronimos monastery and the Tower of Belem, but the small kingdom strained to hold a world. In 1578 King Sebastian and much of the nobility died at Alcazarquivir in a disastrous Moroccan crusade, leaving the throne to an aged cardinal and then, in 1580, to Philip II of Spain, who united the crowns. Sixty years of Iberian Union cost Portugal colonies and independence until a noble revolt restored national kingship in 1640 under John IV of Braganza. Portugal recovered its empire piecemeal, lost Ceylon and Malabar to the Dutch, and reoriented toward Brazil, whose gold and diamonds financed the eighteenth-century monarchy.

title: The Kingdom of Arles (Second Burgundy)
titleline: The Kingdom of Arles (Second Burgundy) - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Arles, also called the Kingdom of Burgundy, was the medieval kingdom of the lands around the western Alps and the Rhone, Savoy, Provence, the Dauphine, Franche-Comte and western Switzerland. Its origins lay in the partition of the Carolingian world: by the Treaty of Verdun (843) and later divisions, middle-Frankish territories between France and Germany were repeatedly reassembled. Around 888, as Carolingian authority collapsed, Rudolf I of the Guelph family founded the kingdom of Upper Burgundy in the Transjuranian lands, while Provence and the lower Rhone formed Lower Burgundy under Boso of Vienne (879). In 933 the two were united under Rudolf II, forming a single kingdom stretching from the Jura to the Mediterranean.
para2: The second kingdom of Burgundy occupied the strategic spine of western Europe: the Alpine passes that linked Italy and Germany and the Rhone corridor that linked the Mediterranean to the north. Its rulers profited from, and were squeezed by, their greater neighbors. They were frequently kingmakers: Hugh of Arles was king of Italy (926-947), and Adelaide of Burgundy married Otto I of Germany. But the kingdom lacked a capital, a common law and a strong fiscal base, and its kings, Rudolf III chief among them, gradually lost control of the church lands and counties to local nobles and bishops. The German kings, holding Italy through the Alpine routes, could not allow the passes to fall into hostile hands.
para3: Rudolf III, childless, named the German king Henry II as his heir, and on Rudolf's death in 1032 the kingdom passed to Henry's Salian successor Conrad II after a brief war. From 1033 the kingdom of Arles was part of the Holy Roman Empire, its crown one of the Empire's three, with Germany and Italy. Imperial control was nominal: Provence drifted toward the French orbit and passed to the Angevins in 1246, the Dauphine was sold to the French heir in 1349, and the counts of Savoy grew into a great power of their own. Emperors were still occasionally crowned king of Arles at Arles or Lyons, Frederick Barbarossa among them in 1178.
para4: By the later Middle Ages the kingdom had dissolved in practice. France absorbed the left bank of the Rhone, Savoy monopolized the Alps, and the Free County of Burgundy, Franche-Comte, passed by marriage to the Valois dukes of Burgundy in 1369 and with them into the Habsburg inheritance after 1477. Only Switzerland escaped the pattern: the confederation founded in the Arlesian lands of the Empire won practical independence by 1499 and recognition at Westphalia. The Kingdom of Arles thus disappeared into the map of Europe, but it is the ancestor of the Rhone valley's contested politics and the reason imperial, French and Italian spheres met where they did.

title: The Western Schism
titleline: The Western Schism - The History Web
para1: The Western Schism (1378-1417) split Latin Christendom between rival popes for forty years. Its origins lay in the 'Avignon Papacy' (1309-1377), when seven French popes governed the church from Avignon under the shadow of the French crown. When Gregory XI returned to Rome in 1377 and died the next year, a Roman mob demanded a Roman pope; the cardinals elected the Neapolitan Urban VI, then, alienated by his harshness, fled to Anagni, declared the election invalid, and chose the French Clement VII, who returned to Avignon. Europe now had two popes, each excommunicating the other, each with his own cardinals, court, taxes and appointments.
para2: Christendom divided along political lines: France, Scotland, Castile, Aragon and Naples backed Avignon; England, most of the Empire, Hungary, Scandinavia and northern Italy backed Rome. The scandal damaged the papacy beyond measure. Two rival hierarchies meant disputed bishoprics, double taxation and cancelled crusades, and the spectacle of vicars of Christ damning each other fed calls for reform from Wyclif in England and Hus in Bohemia. As each line elected successors, Boniface IX and Benedict XIII among them, negotiated reunions repeatedly collapsed, and many concluded that only a general council, superior even to a pope, could end the schism.
para3: In 1409 cardinals of both obediences met at Pisa, deposed both popes, and elected a third, Alexander V; since neither deposed pope accepted the verdict, there were now three lines of popes at once. The breakthrough came at the Council of Constance (1414-1418), summoned by the emperor-elect Sigismund. The Pisan pope John XXIII was deposed, the Roman Gregory XII voluntarily resigned, and the Avignon Benedict XIII, abandoned even by Spain, refused to resign and was deposed in 1417. In November 1417 the council unanimously elected Oddone Colonna as Martin V, accepted across the Latin world, and the schism was over.
para4: Constance also burned Jan Hus at the stake in 1415, and his death ignited the Hussite movement in Bohemia, and asserted that a general council held authority from Christ over the church, a claim popes soon fought to roll back. Under Martin V and Eugenius IV the restored papacy rebuilt its monarchy and defeated the conciliar movement at Basel. But the schism's damage endured: the prestige of the papal office never fully recovered, national churches had grown used to bargaining with Rome, and the demand for 'reform in head and members', deferred once again, would return with far greater force a century later.

title: The County of Flanders
titleline: The County of Flanders - The History Web
para1: The County of Flanders (862-1529) began when the Carolingian king Charles the Bald granted the region to Baldwin 'Iron Arm'. Its early counts expanded methodically at the expense of their neighbors, annexing the coast south to Artois and the lands across the Scheldt in the Empire, so that Flanders straddled the frontier between France and the Holy Roman Empire, its counts vassals of two crowns. The counts protected the abbeys and the growing trade along the coast.
para2: From the 12th century Flanders became the workshop of northern Europe. Flemish towns, Bruges, Ghent, Ypres, turned English wool into the finest cloth of the age, and Bruges and Ghent grew into the richest commercial cities of the north, their weavers and fullers famous and their yearly fairs drawing the trade of Europe. Wealth bred independence: the great communes won charters of self-government and militias of craftsmen that could defeat kings, as at the Battle of the Golden Spurs (1302), where the Flemish urban infantry destroyed the flower of French chivalry at Courtrai. The tension between the counts, backed by France, and the proud towns ran through Flemish history, exploding in revolts under leaders like the Arteveldes of Ghent during the Hundred Years' War.
para3: In 1369 the heiress Margaret of Flanders married Philip the Bold, duke of Burgundy, and in 1384 Flanders passed to the Valois dukes of Burgundy. Under them Flanders was the economic heart of the Burgundian composite state: Bruges and then Antwerp handled its trade, and Flemish art, the brothers van Eyck, Memling, van der Goes, and Flemish music became the glory of the Burgundian court. The towns still fought for their privileges; Bruges was humbled by Philip the Good in 1440, and Ghent rose repeatedly against Maximilian of Habsburg.
para4: Through Mary of Burgundy's marriage Flanders passed to the Habsburgs in 1482, then to their Spanish branch; by the Treaties of Senlis (1493) and Cambrai (1529) France renounced its suzerainty, and Flanders became part of the Habsburg Netherlands. In the Dutch Revolt the southern provinces, unlike the north, were reconquered by Spain, and 'Flanders' lived on as the Spanish and then Austrian Netherlands, and eventually as the Flemish half of Belgium. The medieval county left a double legacy: the urban culture of self-governing towns that shaped the Low Countries, and an artistic tradition that made Flanders a byword for painting.

title: Gaelic Ireland: Kings, Clans and Tara
titleline: Gaelic Ireland: Kings, Clans and Tara - The History Web
para1: Gaelic Ireland. Early medieval Ireland was a world without a capital or a crown that ruled the whole island. Power belonged to perhaps a hundred and fifty petty kingdoms, the tuatha, each a people and a territory bound together by kinship, cattle and oath. Tuatha gathered into overkingdoms, and above them stood the great provincial kingships of Ulster, Munster, Leinster, Connacht and Meath, while at Tara in Meath the High Kings held a sacral kingship whose reach was more honor than administration. Society was ordered by fine, the extended kin-group that shared land, liability and vengeance, and by clientship, in which a lord granted cattle in return for rent and service.
para2: What held this patchwork together was not government but law and learning. The brehons, a hereditary class of jurists, kept one of the oldest legal traditions in Europe, the Brehon law, preserved in tracts like the Senchas Mar. It was a law of compensation rather than punishment: murder, injury and insult were priced in cattle and silver according to rank, from king to poet to commoner. Poets, the filid, formed a learned caste of their own, keepers of genealogy, praise and satire, whose words could raise a king or ruin his name. Irish was a written literary language centuries before most of western Europe wrote in its own tongue.
para3: The economy was pastoral to its core. Wealth was counted in cattle, and the cattle raid was a heroic institution, immortalized in the Tain Bo Cuailnge, the great epic of the Ulster Cycle, where Queen Medb of Connacht marches to steal the Brown Bull of Cooley. Ringforts, raths and crannogs, tens of thousands of which still mark the Irish landscape, were the farmsteads of kings and commoners alike. People lived in scattered farmsteads rather than towns; Ireland had no true towns until the Vikings built them.
para4: Gaelic society proved stubbornly durable. It absorbed the Christianity of the fifth century, the Viking towns of the ninth and tenth, and even the Norman lords of the twelfth, who famously grew more Irish than the Irish themselves. English statute law fought it for centuries, and still the tuatha, the brehons and the poets endured in much of the island until the Tudor conquest and the Flight of the Earls finally broke the old order in the early seventeenth century.

title: Monastic Ireland: Saints and Scholars
titleline: Monastic Ireland: Saints and Scholars - The History Web
para1: Monastic Ireland. Christianity reached Ireland in the fifth century, traditionally with the mission of Patrick in 432, and it took root in a society without cities or Roman institutions. The Irish Church grew around monasteries rather than bishops' seats, and the monastery became the island's town, school, workshop and sanctuary all at once. Great houses like Clonmacnoise on the Shannon, Glendalough in the Wicklow hills, Kells, Armagh and Durrow gathered hundreds of monks, students, farmers and craftsmen around a saint's grave and a abbot's rule.
para2: These monasteries made Ireland, in the phrase of the age, an island of saints and scholars. Irish scribes copied the Gospels and the Latin classics in a distinctive hand, decorating them with knotwork, spirals and interlaced beasts drawn from older Celtic metalwork. The masterpieces of this art - the Book of Kells, the Book of Durrow, the Lindisfarne Gospels made by Irish-trained monks - are among the supreme achievements of medieval Europe. Irish scholars kept Greek learning alive when it had faded in the West, and the monks of Bangor and Clonard taught students from Britain and the continent.
para3: Irish monks also went out as pilgrims and missionaries. Columba founded Iona off Scotland in 563, from which much of northern Britain was converted; Columbanus carried the Irish rule to Gaul and Italy, founding Luxeuil and Bobbio. The austere hermitage of Skellig Michael, perched on a sea-rock off Kerry, shows the other pole of the movement: withdrawal into the Atlantic wilderness. It was Irish monks, too, who taught the Anglo-Saxons at Lindisfarne, seeding the Northumbrian golden age.
para4: The Viking raids of the ninth and tenth centuries burned many great houses and scattered their treasures, and the twelfth-century reform of the Irish Church, capped by the Synod of Kells in 1152, brought Ireland into line with the diocesan structure of continental Christendom. The old monasteries gave way to continental orders, but their legacy endured: a manuscript art without equal, and a memory of learning that became central to Irish identity.

title: Viking Dublin and the Norse Towns of Ireland
titleline: Viking Dublin and the Norse Towns of Ireland - The History Web
para1: Viking Dublin. The first Viking longships appeared off Ireland in 795, when raiders fell on the island monasteries of Rathlin, Inishmurray and Iona. For a generation the Norsemen came to plunder: monasteries, rich in gold vessels and stored food, were their favorite targets, and the annals of the ninth century read as a roll of burned churches and carried-off shrines. Irish kings, endlessly at war with each other, sometimes allied with the raiders against their rivals, and so the strangers were drawn into Irish politics almost at once.
para2: In 841 the Vikings wintered for the first time at Dublin, fortifying a longphort where the River Poddle met the Liffey - at Dubh Linn, the black pool. The raiding base became a town, and the town became a kingdom. Norse Dublin grew rich on trade: slaves above all, but also silver, furs, wine and walrus ivory, linking Ireland to a commercial world that ran from Scandinavia to Byzantium. The Vikings gave Ireland its first true towns - Dublin, Waterford, Wexford, Limerick and Cork were all Norse foundations - and its first coinage, minted in Dublin around 997.
para3: The high point of Norse power came under kings like Olaf Guthfrithson, who in the 930s ruled Dublin and York together. The turning of the tide is traditionally fixed at the Battle of Clontarf in 1014, when the aged High King Brian Boru broke a Dublin-Leinster army at the cost of his own life. The tale is more tangled than the legend - Irishmen fought on both sides - but after Clontarf the Norse towns steadily lost independence and became prizes fought over by Irish kings.
para4: The Norse towns survived their conquerors. Dublin remained the richest port in Ireland, which is why both the last High Kings and the Norman invaders of 1169 made it their first objective. Excavations at Wood Quay have uncovered entire streets of the Viking town, and the Norse legacy runs quietly through Irish life: in coastal place-names like Howth and Wexford, in words for ships and trade, and in the very existence of the capital city itself.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: The Vikings in Ireland

title: The Norman Invasion of Ireland
titleline: The Norman Invasion of Ireland - The History Web
para1: The Norman Invasion of Ireland. The conquest began as a private venture. In 1166 Diarmait Mac Murchada, the deposed king of Leinster, crossed the sea to beg help from King Henry II of England, and received permission to recruit among the Norman lords of Wales. In 1169 and 1170 their advance parties landed in Wexford: mail-clad knights and Welsh archers, led above all by Richard de Clare, called Strongbow. They took Waterford and Dublin, married Mac Murchada's daughter to Strongbow, and when Mac Murchada died in 1171, Strongbow claimed Leinster itself.
para2: That was more than Henry II could allow. A subject building a kingdom across the Irish Sea was a threat, so in October 1171 Henry landed near Waterford with a great fleet and four thousand men - the first King of England to set foot in Ireland. The Norman adventurers submitted their conquests to him, and one Irish king after another came in to offer fealty. Henry granted Meath to his own baron, confirmed the Normans in Leinster, and sailed home leaving a royal governor in Dublin. What had begun as a mercenary adventure had become an English lordship.
para3: The conquest had a veneer of legality: the papal bull Laudabiliter, issued decades earlier by the English pope Adrian IV, was read as authorizing Henry to reform the Irish Church, and at the Synod of Cashel in 1172 the Irish bishops accepted his overlordship. The Normans brought castles - the great stone keeps at Trim and Carrickfergus - and carved eastern Ireland into feudal lordships, while the west remained under Gaelic kings who paid tribute and went their own way.
para4: The settlement of 1169-1172 set the pattern for eight centuries: an English administration seated in Dublin, an area of direct control that shrank and grew, and a Gaelic Ireland that was never wholly subdued. The Lordship of Ireland born in those years lasted until 1542, when Henry VIII raised it into a kingdom. Every later chapter of the Irish story - plantations, penal laws, union and independence - runs back to Strongbow's archers at Baginbun, where, as the old rhyme had it, Ireland was lost and won.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Lordship of Ireland

title: The Lordship of Ireland and the Pale
titleline: The Lordship of Ireland and the Pale - The History Web
para1: The Lordship of Ireland. From 1171 the kings of England were Lords of Ireland, ruling through a justiciar and a council seated in Dublin. But the lordship was never a conquest completed. The Norman barons - de Burghs in Connacht, FitzGeralds in Kildare and Desmond, Butlers in Ormond - built their castles and carved out liberties in which they were kings in all but name, while beyond the frontier the Gaelic chiefs, O'Neills in Ulster, O'Briens in Thomond, MacCarthys in Desmond, held their lands by their own ancient law. Medieval Ireland was a checkerboard of Englishry and Irishry.
para2: The lordship's high water mark came early: by 1300 most of the island acknowledged Dublin's writ. Then the tide turned. The Bruce invasion of 1315-1318, when Edward Bruce landed with a Scottish army and had himself proclaimed King of Ireland, burned through the colony and proved it could not defend itself. Famine followed, then the Black Death, which fell hardest on the English towns. Gaelic chiefs recovered their lands, and the settler families beyond the frontier turned native, adopting the Irish language, dress and fosterage until the statutes complained they were more Irish than the Irish themselves.
para3: Parliament answered with the Statutes of Kilkenny in 1366, forbidding the English of Ireland to marry the Irish, speak their language or use their law - the first great codification of the two nations on one island. They changed little on the ground. By the fifteenth century the area of secure English rule had shrunk to the Pale, a fortified strip around Dublin, defended by dykes and watch-towers; the rest of the island paid the Dublin government only an occasional black rent, protection money in reverse.
para4: The fifteenth-century lordship became a pawn in English dynastic wars, dominated by the great earls of Kildare, who ruled as Lords Deputy almost as hereditary kings - until 1534, when Silken Thomas FitzGerald's rebellion gave Henry VIII the excuse to end their power. The failure of the medieval lordship convinced the Tudors that Ireland had to be conquered outright, and so the loose, fading medieval arrangement was replaced by a kingdom, a standing army and plantations.

title: The Picts and the Birth of Alba
titleline: The Picts and the Birth of Alba - The History Web
para1: The Picts and the Birth of Alba. North of the Roman wall lay the people the Romans called Picti, the painted ones. The Picts were not one tribe but a confederation of peoples of northern and eastern Scotland, farmers and formidable warriors who had broken Roman expeditions and, in 685, destroyed a Northumbrian army at Dun Nechtain, one of the great battles of early Britain. They left no writings of their own, but they left their art: hundreds of carved stones incised with the enigmatic Pictish symbols - beasts, mirrors, combs and crescents - and later cross-slabs of breathtaking workmanship, and hoards of silver like the treasure of St Ninian's Isle.
para2: Pictish kingship passed not from father to son but, most scholars hold, through the mother's line, a system that kept the crown moving between kindreds. Pictland was divided into great provinces, each with its own mormaer, and the overking ruled from fortresses like Burghead and Dunnottar. Conversion came in the sixth and seventh centuries, traditionally through Columba of Iona, and the Pictish church with its monasteries at St Andrews and Dunkeld became a partner of the kings.
para3: West of the Picts, in Argyll, stood Dal Riata, the kingdom of the Scots - Gaelic speakers whose kindred spanned the North Channel to Antrim in Ireland. For centuries Picts and Scots fought, married and traded. Then, in the ninth century, under pressure from Viking assaults that shattered both peoples, the two crowns united: Kenneth mac Alpin, king of Dal Riata, took the Pictish throne about 843, and his descendants ruled a merged realm that called itself Alba.
para4: The union was the birth of Scotland. The Pictish language and symbols faded away, absorbed into Gaelic culture so completely that historians still argue over how, while the kingship of Alba moved its heart to Scone, where Scottish kings were inaugurated on the Stone of Destiny. When Macbeth and later Malcolm III ruled in the eleventh century, they were kings of a Gaelic-speaking Alba that reached from the Mounth to the Forth - the core of the kingdom to come.

title: Dal Riata and the Gaelic West
titleline: Dal Riata and the Gaelic West - The History Web
para1: Dal Riata. Around the year 500, give or take a generation, Gaelic-speaking Scots from the Antrim coast of Ireland planted a kingdom in the sea-girt peninsula of Argyll, in what is now western Scotland. The kingdom of Dal Riata faced two ways at once: its boats crossed the narrow North Channel in hours, and for centuries its kings, kindreds and churchmen moved freely between the Irish and Scottish shores, treating the sea not as a border but as a road. Its heartlands were the rocky stronghold of Dunadd, the ridge-fort of Dunollie, and the islands of the Inner Hebrides.
para2: Dal Riata was a maritime warrior society, divided among four great kindreds, and its kings led war-bands by sea against the Picts to the east, the Britons of Strathclyde, and their Irish cousins across the water. The annals record sea-battles and cattle-tribute; its warriors fought as far afield as the Orkneys. The kingdom's place in the power politics of the north was settled at the Convention of Druim Cett in 575, where the Irish over-king and the Dal Riatan king Aedan mac Gabrain divided their obligations: the Scottish Dal Riata would serve its own king, the Irish Dal Riata its own.
para3: The kingdom's lasting fame is holy. In 563 Columba - Colum Cille - an Irish prince of the northern Ui Neill, came to Dal Riata and received the island of Iona. The monastery he founded there became the spiritual capital of the Gaelic west: from Iona went the missionaries who converted the Picts and taught the Northumbrians at Lindisfarne, and on Iona, most scholars believe, the scribes began the Book of Kells. The abbots of Iona for generations outranked bishops, and the island remained the burial place of kings - Scottish, Irish and even Norse.
para4: Viking assault in the ninth century broke the sea-kingdom's world: Iona was burned and its monks martyred, and the Dal Riatan throne passed, through Kenneth mac Alpin, into union with the Picts. But Dal Riata's legacy was the greater one. It had carried the Gaelic language, the name Scot, and the Christian faith into mainland Scotland - so completely that the united kingdom of Alba thought of itself as Scottish, and the land of the Picts took its name from the Irish sea-kingdom on its western shore.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Book of Kells

title: The Wars of Scottish Independence
titleline: The Wars of Scottish Independence - The History Web
para1: The Wars of Scottish Independence. In 1286 King Alexander III of Scotland died in a fall from his horse, and his only heir, the child Margaret, the Maid of Norway, died on the voyage to her kingdom in 1290. With the succession in ruins, Scotland's guardians asked Edward I of England to judge between the claimants. Edward chose John Balliol - and then treated him as a vassal, hearing appeals from his courts and summoning him like a servant. When the Scots defied him and allied with France in 1295, Edward invaded, sacked Berwick with terrible slaughter, deposed Balliol, and carried off the Stone of Destiny from Scone.
para2: Scotland would not submit. In 1297 William Wallace, a knight of no great family, rose in arms, and with Andrew Murray destroyed an English army at Stirling Bridge. Edward answered in person and crushed Wallace at Falkirk in 1298; Wallace fought on as a fugitive until he was betrayed, taken to London, and hanged, drawn and quartered in 1305. Into the breach stepped Robert the Bruce, Earl of Carrick, who in 1306 killed his chief rival John Comyn in a Dumfries church and had himself crowned at Scone. Defeated and driven into hiding, he returned to wage a guerrilla war, castle by castle, until only Stirling held out.
para3: The deliverance came at Bannockburn, in June 1314. Edward II marched north with one of the greatest armies England had ever raised, and Bruce met it on ground of his choosing, where streams and bogs broke the charge of the English knights. In two days of fighting the schiltrons of Scottish spearmen drove the flower of English chivalry into the Bannock Burn; Edward fled, and English power in Scotland collapsed. It was, as the Scots said, the day the kingdom was won back.
para4: War dragged on: Scottish raiders harried northern England, and in 1320 the Scottish barons sent the Declaration of Arbroath to the Pope, proclaiming that they fought not for glory or riches but for freedom alone. Pope John XXII recognized Robert as king, and in 1328 the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton saw England renounce all claim to overlordship. Scotland had kept its independence - the only kingdom in the British Isles, beside England itself, to survive the Middle Ages unconquered.
source4label: National Records of Scotland: Declaration of Arbroath 700th Anniversary Booklet

title: The Stewart Dynasty
titleline: The Stewart Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Stewart Dynasty. The Stewarts took their name from office: they were hereditary High Stewards of Scotland, stewards of the royal household, raised to the highest nobility for their part in the wars of independence. In 1315 Walter the Steward married Marjorie, daughter of Robert the Bruce, and when her son succeeded David II in 1371, Robert II became the first Stewart king. His line would hold the Scottish throne for more than three centuries - and eventually the English and Irish thrones as well.
para2: Few royal houses endured such a run of calamity. Robert III was broken by injury and intrigue; James I was murdered by his own nobles in 1437; James II was killed by the bursting of his own cannon; James III died after the Battle of Sauchieburn, fighting rebels who had crowned his son; and James IV fell at Flodden in 1513, the last British king to die in battle, with the flower of his nobility around him. Again and again a child inherited the crown, and the kingdom was governed by regents and rival factions through long minorities.
para3: Yet the dynasty built. The Stewarts founded universities - St Andrews in 1413, Glasgow in 1451, Aberdeen in 1495 - patronized the great makars of Scots poetry, and under James IV maintained a court famous across Europe, with a navy whose flagship, the Great Michael, was the largest ship afloat. They ground down the semi-independent Lordship of the Isles, bringing the Gaelic west under the crown, and married their way into the politics of Europe: James V's French marriages bound Scotland to the old alliance with France.
para4: The sixteenth century brought the reckoning. James V died leaving a week-old daughter, Mary, Queen of Scots, whose turbulent reign ended in forced abdication and flight to England. Her son James VI, raised amid Reformation and faction, proved the ablest of his line; and when Elizabeth of England died childless in 1603, he inherited her crown as well. The Stewarts - by then spelled Stuart - had risen from stewards to kings of the whole British Isles.

title: The Welsh Kingdoms and the Marcher Lords
titleline: The Welsh Kingdoms and the Marcher Lords - The History Web
para1: The Welsh Kingdoms. When the Anglo-Saxons took the lowlands of Britain, the Britons of the west kept their hills. Medieval Wales was never one realm but a family of kingdoms - Gwynedd in the mountains of the northwest, Powys in the east, Deheubarth in the southwest - whose princes warred with the English, with each other, and within their own houses, for Welsh law divided a man's inheritance among all his sons, and every succession was a contest. Yet the Welsh shared one language, one law - the code of Hywel Dda, the tenth-century king who ruled most of Wales - and one fierce sense of being the true Britons, the old people of the island.
para2: The Norman tide broke on the Welsh border. After 1066 the English kings planted barons along the frontier - the March, from Chester to Chepstow - and these Marcher lords conquered what they could hold, building the mightiest castles in Britain and ruling their lordships like little kings, with their own courts and armies, owing the crown little more than loyalty. Against them the Welsh princes fought a long, grinding war of raid and revolt, and slowly the balance turned: the twelfth and thirteenth centuries saw the rise of native principality, above all in Gwynedd.
para3: Under Llywelyn the Great and his grandson Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, Gwynedd forced the other Welsh dynasties and even the Marchers to accept its leadership. In 1267 Henry III of England, by the Treaty of Montgomery, acknowledged Llywelyn ap Gruffudd as Prince of Wales - the first and last native prince formally to bear the title. It was the high point of Welsh independence, and it lasted fifteen years.
para4: Edward I ended it. His armies overran Gwynedd in 1277 and again in 1282-83; Llywelyn was killed in a skirmish at Cilmeri, and his brother Dafydd was captured and executed. Edward ringed Snowdonia with the greatest castle-building program of the Middle Ages - Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech, Beaumaris, today a World Heritage Site - and by the Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284 annexed the principality to the English crown. Wales would rise once more under Owain Glyndwr, but the age of the native princes had ended at Cilmeri.
source2label: UNESCO: Castles of King Edward in Gwynedd

title: Owain Glyndwr's Rebellion
titleline: Owain Glyndwr's Rebellion - The History Web
para1: Owain Glyndwr's Rebellion. Owain Glyndwr was no landless rebel but a descendant of the princes of Powys, a gentleman educated in English law at the Inns of Court, who had fought in the armies of Richard II. In 1400 a dispute with his Marcher neighbor, Lord Grey of Ruthin, who had seized his lands and had the king's ear, drove Glyndwr to defiance. On 16 September 1400 his followers proclaimed him Prince of Wales, and the quarrel of one landowner became the last great war of Welsh independence.
para2: The rising spread like fire through Wales. Welsh students left Oxford, Welsh laborers walked home from England, and the guerrilla war was fought from the mountains and forests Glyndwr's men knew and the English did not. In 1402 he captured Lord Grey himself and crushed a Marcher army at Pilleth; in 1404 he took the great castles of Harlech and Aberystwyth and held a Welsh parliament at Machynlleth, where he was crowned with envoys from France, Scotland and Spain in attendance. In 1405 he sealed a formal alliance with France, and French troops landed to fight beside him.
para3: Glyndwr's vision went beyond war. In letters to the French king he proposed an independent Wales with its own church and two universities, one in the north and one in the south - a national program centuries ahead of its time. For a few years a Welsh state existed in fact, with chancery, seal and parliament, holding the west and center of the country while the English clung to the coasts and castles.
para4: It could not last. England under Prince Hal - the future Henry V - ground the rebellion down with blockade and devastation, and the French went home. By 1409 the great castles were retaken; Glyndwr's family was captured; his allies were bought or broken. He himself was never betrayed, never captured, and never pardoned: around 1415 he vanished into the mountains, and no one knows where he lies. Wales remembers him as its last native Prince of Wales and the father of its nationhood.

title: The Heptarchy and the Rise of Wessex
titleline: The Heptarchy and the Rise of Wessex - The History Web
para1: The Heptarchy. After the Roman legions left Britain, the Angles, Saxons and Jutes who settled the island built not one kingdom but many. Historians call the patchwork the Heptarchy, the seven kingdoms: Kent, Sussex and Wessex in the south, Essex and East Anglia in the east, Mercia in the midlands, and Northumbria in the north. In truth there were always more than seven, and the little kingdoms warred, married and swallowed one another for three centuries, each king striving to be bretwalda, the overlord who could exact tribute from the rest.
para2: Supremacy passed from kingdom to kingdom like a torch. Kent under Aethelberht held it first; then Northumbria, whose seventh-century golden age joined military power to the learning of Bede and the art of Lindisfarne. In the eighth century the torch passed to Mercia: King Offa (757-796) treated with Charlemagne as an equal, minted fine coin, and threw up Offa's Dyke, the great earthwork along the Welsh border that still bears his name. Each supremacy was personal, and died with the man who held it.
para3: Then came the Vikings. The Great Heathen Army that landed in 865 destroyed East Anglia and Northumbria, overran Mercia, and by 878 had driven the last free English king, Alfred of Wessex, into the marshes of Athelney. Alfred's survival changed the fate of England. From Athelney he came back to win at Edington, pen the Danes behind the Danelaw, and rebuild his kingdom on fortified burhs, a reformed army and a revival of learning.
para4: Alfred's children and grandchildren finished the work. Edward the Elder and his warrior sister Aethelflaed, Lady of the Mercians, rolled up the Danelaw burh by burh, and in 927 Athelstan took York and was acknowledged as king of all the English - and, for a moment, overlord of Britain after his crushing victory at Brunanburh in 937. The seven kingdoms had become one: England. Wessex had risen from a southern shire to the royal house of a united nation, and its line would hold the throne until the Normans came.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Wessex

title: Alfred the Great and the Danelaw
titleline: Alfred the Great and the Danelaw - The History Web
para1: Alfred the Great and the Danelaw. When Alfred became King of Wessex in 871, the Viking Great Army had already destroyed every other English kingdom, and Wessex itself stood on the edge. In the winter of 878 a Danish surprise attack drove him into the Somerset marshes, where, the chroniclers say, he sheltered at Athelney, burned the peasant's cakes, and gathered his strength. In May he came out of the marsh, raised the levies of three shires, and broke the Danish army at Edington. The Danish leader Guthrum accepted baptism and withdrew to rule the conquered north and east - the territory that became the Danelaw.
para2: Alfred spent the rest of his reign making sure it could never happen again. He ringed his kingdom with burhs, fortified market towns planned on grids - Winchester, Oxford, Wallingford, Wareham - garrisoned and placed so that no part of Wessex lay more than a day's march from refuge. He divided his army so that half was always in the field, and built longships of his own design to meet the raiders at sea. When the last great Viking army came in the 890s, it found a kingdom that could not be broken, and gave up.
para3: What made Alfred unique among warrior kings was that he fought for the mind as well. Lamenting that learning had collapsed with the monasteries, he gathered scholars to his court and himself translated the essential books into Old English: Boethius, Augustine, Gregory the Great, and Bede's history. He began the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, the first continuous national history in a European vernacular, and issued a law code joined to the laws of his ancestors. He is the only English king called the Great, and he earned it in the schoolroom as much as on the battlefield.
para4: The Danelaw outlasted its conquerors: for two centuries eastern England lived under Danish law, its towns - Derby, Leicester, Lincoln, Nottingham, Stamford - and its place-names ending in -by and -thorpe still marking the settlement. But Alfred's kingdom endured, and his house united England. His grandson Athelstan was the first king of all the English, and Alfred's burhs, laws and chronicle became the foundations of the English state.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Alfred the Great

title: The Norman Conquest of England
titleline: The Norman Conquest of England - The History Web
para1: The Norman Conquest. On 5 January 1066 Edward the Confessor, King of England, died childless, and the witan chose Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex, the most powerful man in the kingdom. Across the Channel, Duke William of Normandy claimed that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to support him. Harold swore anyway - on sacred relics, the Normans said - and William prepared an invasion with the Pope's banner behind him. First, though, another claimant struck: in September the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada landed in the north with Harold's own brother Tostig, and Harold Godwinson force-marched his army to destroy them at Stamford Bridge on 25 September.
para2: Three days later William landed at Pevensey. Harold turned his exhausted army around and marched it two hundred and fifty miles south, meeting the Normans on a ridge near Hastings on 14 October 1066. All day the English shield-wall held against Norman arrows and cavalry; late in the afternoon the feigned retreats drew the English downhill and broke their line, and Harold fell, struck - the Bayeux Tapestry's ambiguous figure suggests - by an arrow and cut down by knights. By Christmas, William was crowned King of England in Westminster Abbey.
para3: Conquest followed coronation. William ground down resistance in the west and north - the Harrying of the North in 1069-70 left Yorkshire a wasteland - and secured his kingdom with castles: within a generation the motte-and-bailey and then the stone keep, from the White Tower of London to Dover, stood over every town of consequence. In 1086 he ordered the survey of his whole kingdom, recorded in Domesday Book, the most complete record any medieval state ever made of itself.
para4: The conquest replaced a ruling class wholesale: by 1086 only a handful of English landowners remained, and Norman French became the language of court, castle and law for three centuries, while English went underground and emerged transformed. England was bound into the politics of France, pulling its kings into continental wars for four hundred years, and its church, law and administration were remade on continental lines. No event in English history cut deeper: a new aristocracy, a new architecture, a new language of power - and the last successful invasion of England.

title: Magna Carta and the Barons' Wars
titleline: Magna Carta and the Barons' Wars - The History Web
para1: Magna Carta. King John of England lost an empire and broke a kingdom. By 1204 he had lost Normandy to the King of France, and for a decade he taxed, fined and bullied his barons to pay for its recovery - until the defeat at Bouvines in 1214 destroyed his last army and his credit. In the spring of 1215 the barons of the north renounced their homage, took London, and forced the king to meet them in the meadow of Runnymede. There, on 15 June 1215, John set his seal to the Great Charter: sixty-three clauses that bound the king himself to the law.
para2: Most of the charter dealt with the grievances of the moment - reliefs, wardships, forest law, the abuses of royal officials. Buried among them were clauses 39 and 40: no free man was to be taken, imprisoned or dispossessed except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land, and to no one would the king sell, deny or delay right or justice. In those two sentences later generations found the foundation of due process of law, and of the principle that the ruler stands under the law, not above it.
para3: As a peace treaty the charter failed within weeks. John had it annulled by the Pope, the barons called in Prince Louis of France, and England plunged into the First Barons' War. When John died in October 1216, his nine-year-old son Henry III was crowned with the charter reissued in his name - the proof that the idea was bigger than the quarrel. The war ended at Lincoln and Sandwich in 1217, and Magna Carta, confirmed again in 1225, became the settled law of the land.
para4: The charter's logic kept working. Baronial reform under Simon de Montfort forced the Provisions of Oxford on Henry III, and when that failed, the Second Barons' War ended at Evesham in 1265, with Montfort dead but his parliament - the first to summon townsmen beside knights - remembered as a model. Edward I confirmed the charter in 1297, and four of the sixty-three clauses, including the two great ones, remain on England's statute book today. From Runnymede run straight lines to the Petition of Right, the Bill of Rights, and the Fifth Amendment.

title: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381
titleline: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 - The History Web
para1: The Peasants' Revolt. A generation after the Black Death carried off perhaps half of England, the survivors found their labor precious and their prospects rising - and their lords determined to hold them down. The Statute of Labourers froze wages, the lawyers of the manor dug up old dues, and villeinage, the bondage of the unfree peasant to his lord, was enforced more harshly as it became less bearable. Into this resentment the government of the boy-king Richard II dropped three poll taxes in four years, and the third, in 1380, fell on every adult in the realm, rich and poor alike.
para2: In May 1381 the tax collectors came to Essex, and Essex refused to pay. The revolt spread through Kent, where the rebels freed the itinerant preacher John Ball from prison - his rhyme, when Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman, became the slogan of the rising - and chose as their captain Wat Tyler, perhaps an old soldier. On 12 June the Essex and Kentish men, tens of thousands strong, camped on Blackheath outside London, and the next day sympathizers opened the city to them.
para3: For three days London was theirs. The rebels burned the Savoy, John of Gaunt's great palace, opened the prisons, beheaded the Lord Chancellor and the Lord Treasurer on Tower Hill, and met the fourteen-year-old king twice in parley. At Mile End, Richard granted them charters of freedom and pardon, and most of the Essex men went home believing they had won. At Smithfield the next day, in the middle of a tense negotiation, the Lord Mayor of London suddenly cut Wat Tyler down, and the rebel army wavered, bows half-drawn - until the boy-king rode forward alone and told them: I am your captain, follow me.
para4: It was a rescue, not a surrender. Once the danger passed, the charters were revoked - villeins you are and villeins you shall remain, Richard told the suppliants of Essex - and the rebel leaders were hunted down and hanged. Yet the revolt had burned itself into the mind of the governing class: no poll tax was attempted again for six hundred years, and villeinage, broken in practice, faded away within a generation. The rebels of 1381 lost every battle but the last one.
